title: 第三章　灵魂的实验室

children: 1893年，生活在圣彼得堡的年轻贵族、有抱负的外交官马夫里基·法比阿诺维奇·席林（Mavriky Fabianovich Shilling）在日记中写道，他跑遍了商店寻找带锁的厚笔记本，但都卖光了，他能做的只有订购一个。在苏联俄罗斯，这种制作精良、配有锁和钥匙的日记本通常是买不到的。斯大林时代的日记作者不得不使用学校练习本，即便如此也供应短缺。许多日记作者提到，由于缺乏纸张和笔记本，他们不得不暂停撰写编年史。《真理报》的一篇文章哀叹学校笔记本的短缺及其低劣的质量：“粗糙劣质、颜色不明的封面容易吸附污垢，因此显得脏乱不堪。墨渍和涂抹的词语比一年级小学生所能允许的还要多，而这并不能怪孩子们。”没有笔记本时，一些日记作者便在账本上写作，这些账本或许是他们在工作场所找到的。
使用账本似乎启发了工会官员亚历山大·梅德韦德科夫（Alexander Medvedkov），使他产生了一种独特的日记式记账法。他在几张表格中记录了他生活中每一天的事件，其子标题包括“日期”“星期”“所做工作与休息的名称”“工作与休息的内容”“浪费的时间”以及“私密生活”。在表格中，他记录了每天花在某项活动上的小时数。另一位日记作者则写在印有苏联时期或革命前官方抬头的散页信笺上。
因此，斯大林时代的日记在外观上与革命前的日记形成了鲜明的对比，后一类日记更多写在厚实、有时是皮面的精制纸张册子里。对于那些跨越革命分界线写作、且在某个时刻不得不放弃精装本而改用苏联政权生产的粗糙笔记本的日记作者来说，这种对比显得更加强烈。
这一形象——皮面册子和学校笔记本——象征着日记作者从有序的生活被猛烈推入贫困和动荡状态的方式，同时也概括了另一种转变：从日记作为社会特权成员的追求，转向全民识字、学校教育和自我记录的民主化议程。

In 1893 Mavriky Fabianovich Shilling, a young nobleman and aspiring diplomat living in St. Petersburg, noted in his diary that he had scoured the stores to find a thick notebook with a lock, but they were sold out and all he could do was place an order. Such diaries, elaborately crafted and equipped with lock and key, were generally un-available in Soviet Russia. Stalin-era diarists had to make do with school exercise books, and even those were in short supply. Many diarists mentioned that for lack of paper and notebooks they had to suspend the writing of their chronicles. An article in Pravda bemoaned the shortages of school notebooks and their low quality: “The rough and coarse covers of indeterminate color easily absorb dirt and are therefore soiled and untidy. There are many more blots and smeared words than would be permissible even for first-graders, and the children are not to blame for this.” In the absence of notebooks some diarists wrote in account books they presumably found at their workplaces.

Using an account book seem to have inspired Alexander Medvedkov, a trade union official, to an idiosyncratic form of diaristic bookkeeping. He recorded the events of each day of his life in several tables, with such subheadings as “date,” “day of the week,” “designation of performed work and rest,” “content of work and rest,” “wasted time,” and “intimacy.” In the tables he recorded the number of hours spent on a given activity each day. Another diarist wrote on loose sheets of official stationery that bore both Soviet and prerevolutionary letterheads.

Stalin-era diaries thus contrast sharply in outward appearance with diaries from prerevolutionary times, which were more often kept in thick, sometimes leather-bound, volumes made of finely grained paper. This contrast is put in even sharper relief in the case of diarists who wrote across the revolutionary divide and at some point had to abandon their bound volumes for the coarse notebooks produced by the Soviet regime.

Emblematic of the way diarists were jolted from orderly lives into a state of impoverishment and violent upheaval, the image of the two books—leather volume and school notebook—also encapsulates another transition: from diary-keeping as a pursuit of privileged members of society to a democratic agenda of universal literacy, schooling, and recording of the self.

20世纪30年代日记作者不得不应对的纸张短缺，反而凸显了他们内心动笔写作的冲动。同样的紧迫感也反映在他们日记中一系列共同的主题上，他们将这些主题表达为紧迫的任务和需要参与、奋斗并最终解决的问题。许多日记作者相信他们生活在一个历史性的时代，并力求参与其发展过程。无论是斯大林政权的忠实支持者，还是某些直言不讳的批评者，都同样把参与历史进程看作不容置疑的义务；对许多人来说，这也是他们的愿望。这些日记作者也知道，要参与革命的转型政治，他们必须首先改造自己。他们利用日记，根据“社会用途”的任务来监控自己的思想和表现。要与历史保持一致，需要努力和奋斗。虽然许多作者未能始终如一地与革命心灵相通，而是专注于较小的追求（从日常杂务到情感问题），但他们为自己的“琐碎”担忧而自责，并坚持认为他们作为人类和进步公民的价值取决于他们服务于更广泛社会利益的能力。他们努力将自己写进更大集体的经验之中，并把这个集体想象为一个活生生的有机体。在这个意识形态监视严密的时代，归属于集体为他们提供了超越单纯生存的意义和活力。反过来，许多无法或不愿与前进中的集体步调一致的人感到沮丧和无用，有些人记录了自己求死的愿望。革命作为一种创造生命的力量，使那些反对革命国家的人面临生或死的问题。

The paper shortages with which diarists of the 1930s had to contend only underscore the urge they felt to take pen to paper. The same sense of urgency is reflected in a set of shared themes in their diaries, which they voiced as pressing mandates and questions demanding engagement, struggle, and ultimately, resolution. Many diarists believed they were living in a historical epoch, and they strove to participate in its unfolding. The unquestioned duty and, for many, desire to become involved in the march of history took hold in equal measure of loyal supporters of the Stalinist regime and of some its vocal critics. These diarists also knew that to participate in a revolutionary politics of transformation they must first transform themselves. They used their diaries to monitor their thoughts and their performance in light of the mandate of “social use.” To be aligned with history required work and struggle. While many authors failed to commune with the revolution consistently and were instead preoccupied with smaller pursuits, ranging from daily chores to matters of the heart, they blamed themselves for their “petty” concerns and insisted that their value as human beings and progressive citizens depended on their ability to serve the wider interests of society. They strove to write themselves into the experience of a larger collectivity, which they imagined as a living organism. Adherence to the collective promised them meaning and vitality beyond sheer survival in an age of intense ideological surveillance. In turn, many of those who were unable or unwilling to think in step with the marching collective felt depressed and useless, and some recorded their wish to die. A life-creating force, the revolution confronted those who opposed the revolutionary state with a question of life or death.

zh: 革命的时代
en: A Revolutionary Time

children: 20世纪30年代的许多苏联日记都流露出一种强烈的意识，即生活在一个特殊的、历史性的时期，并有义务将其记录下来。“我什么时候才能最终写完关于30年代的回忆录？”一位日记作者问道。事实上，这位作者在1932年（那个十年才刚刚开始）就提出了这个问题，这说明人们已经有了这种观念，即斯大林式的工业化运动是一个正在形成中的独特时代。日记不仅是一个观察者的编年史记录，它还经常承担着将作者写入这个时代的额外任务：在历史语境下建立自我与时代之间的对话，从而将自我提升到历史主体的水平。日记的这种双重目的——既是形成中的历史记录，又是形成中的历史主体自我的记录——定义了这一时期的许多共产主义日记，但它也扩展到了对共产主义政权持批判态度的日记作者身上。事实上，这些作者对政治体制的批评越是直言不讳，他们对历史的诉求就越强烈。

亚历山大·热列兹尼亚科夫（Alexander Zhelezniakov）是一名在沃洛格达地区活跃于集体化运动的共产党人，他在听说自己将被任命为另一个地区村苏维埃主席后开始写日记。在第一篇日记中，他向他的“活动分子”同伴告别。热列兹尼亚科夫详细描述了他们的“斗争”和成就——70%的农户实现了集体化；成功组织了12个集体农庄（kolkhozes）——他写道，这一“胜利必须记录在利克托什斯科耶村苏维埃集体农庄的历史中”。热列兹尼亚科夫将他重新任命的消息嵌入到一个更大的集体阶级斗争叙事中：“阶级敌人富农并未沉睡，煽动落后的贫农和中农群众反对集体农庄……因此，在与过时且垂死的资本主义分子的激烈冲突中，我们的集体农庄诞生、成长并壮大。斗争依然任重道远，尤其是在新的地点，即我被党区委员会调往的皮罗戈夫村苏维埃。”
同样的策略在玛莎·斯科特（Masha Scott）的日记中也清晰可见，她将构建个人生活叙事的意识形态框架扩展到了极限——即国际阶级斗争的史诗。玛莎是住在马格尼托哥尔斯克的一位农民出身的教师，她回忆起与来访的美国工程师约翰·斯科特相遇的情景，两人后来结婚。她描述了见到一个消瘦的年轻人时的印象，他穿着破烂，满身是高炉粉尘：
这是我见过的第一个美国人，他看起来像个无家可归的男孩。我在他身上看到了资本主义压迫的产物。我在脑海中看到了他悲惨的童年；我想象着他还是个男孩时，被迫在某个资本主义工厂里进行的长时间的非人劳动；我想象着他拿到的那点微薄得令人羞愧的工资，只够买面包，以便第二天去干活；我想象着他害怕失去这点微薄的收入，万一他的工作不能让那些寄生虫老板满意并为他们牟利，他就会失业流落街头。

Many Soviet diaries from the 1930s bespeak a strong sense of living in an exceptional, historic period and having an obligation to record it. “When will I finally write my memoirs about the 1930s?” one diarist asked. The fact that this author posed the question in 1932, when the decade had barely begun, illustrates how much of a notion there already existed of the Stalinist industrialization campaign as a distinct epoch in the making. More than just the record of an observing chronicler, the diary frequently had the additional task of writing its author into the age: of creating a dialogue between the self and the age in historical terms, and of thus raising the self to the level of a historical subject. This double purpose of the diary, as a record both of history in the making and of the self as a historical subject in the making, defined many a Communist diary of this period, but it also extended to diarists who critically engaged the Communist regime. The more vocally these diarists criticized the political order, in fact, the more strongly did they appeal to history.

Alexander Zhelezniakov, a Communist active in the collectivization campaign in the Vologda region, began to keep a diary upon hearing that he would be appointed chairman of a village soviet in another district. In the first entry he bade farewell to his fellow “activists.” Detailing their “struggles” and achievements—70 percent of the peasant households collectivized; 12 kolkhozes (collective farms) successfully organized—Zhelezniakov wrote that this “victory must be registered in the history of the kolkhozes of the Likhtoshskoe village soviet.” Zhelezniakov embedded the news of his reappointment in the larger narrative of a collective class struggle: “The class enemy, the kulak, did not sleep, inciting the backward masses of poor peasants and those peasants of average means against the kolkhozes . . . Thus, in a bitter skirmish with the obsolete and dying capitalist elements, our kolkhozes were born, reared, and strengthened. A lot of struggle still lies ahead, especially at the new location, the Pirogov village Soviet, where I have been transferred by the party’s district committee.”

The same strategy is visible in the diary of Masha Scott, who expanded the ideological frame structuring the narration of her personal life to its utmost extent—the epic of international class struggle. Masha, a teacher of peasant background living in Magnitogorsk, re-called meeting John Scott, a visiting American engineer, whom she would later marry. She described her impressions upon seeing an emaciated young man, dressed in rags and covered with blast-furnace dust:

The first American I had ever seen, he looked like a homeless boy. I saw in him the product of capitalist oppression. I saw in my mind’s eye his sad childhood; I imagined the long hours of inhuman labor which he had been forced to perform in some capitalist factory while still a boy; I imagined the shamefully low wages he received, only sufficient to buy enough bread so that he could to go work the next day; I imagined his fear of losing even this pittance and being thrown on the streets unemployed in case he was unable to do his work to the satisfaction and profit of his parasitic bosses.
剧作家弗谢沃洛德·维什涅夫斯基（Vsevolod Vishnevsky）认为记日记是他的“任务”，旨在“为历史保留我们的观察，保留我们现在的观点——即参与者的观点”。通过阅读维什涅夫斯基及其同代人的历史“错误与胜利”，后代人将更加坚定地献身于建设完美的共产主义社会。

即使是一份作者严格构思为日常生活编年史的日记，也具有历史导向。来自加里宁（特维尔）的档案保管员尼古拉·朱拉夫廖夫（Nikolai Zhuravlev）想为未来的城市历史学家和苏联日常生活历史学家创作一份关于“一个正常人生活中的正常[日子]”的连续记录。具有说明意义的是，朱拉夫廖夫在一个不寻常的日子——建城八百周年纪念日——开始了他的平凡生活编年史。朱拉夫廖夫在他的项目中附带了历史意图，这在他对当天阅兵和演讲的记述结论中显而易见：“像这样的庆祝活动只能发生在社会主义土地上！我记得沙皇制度下的那些官方‘节日’……但我们的节日是真正的群众性节日，是真正的人民节日。”他试图记录与以往时代有着质的区别的苏联日常生活，认为这种生活被革命所改变，与斯大林宣称的彻底变革日常生活的说法相称。

The playwright Vsevolod Vishnevsky regarded it as his “task” to keep a diary to “preserve for history our observations, our present point of view—the point of view of the participant.” In reading about the historical “mistakes and victories” of Vishnevsky and his contemporaries future generations would be strengthened in their dedication to build the perfect Communist society.

Even a diary that its author conceived of strictly as a chronicle of everyday life had a historical thrust. Nikolai Zhuravlev, an archivist from Kalinin (Tver), wanted to create a serial record of “normal [days] in the life of a normal person” for the sake of a future historian of the city and of Soviet daily life. Tellingly Zhuravlev began his chronicle of ordinary life on an extraordinary day—the eight hundredth anniversary of the city’s founding. That Zhuravlev attached a historical intention to his project is clear in the conclusion to his account of the day’s parades and speeches: “Celebrations like this can take place only in the land of socialism! I remember these official ‘festivities’ under tsarism . . . But our holiday is a genuine mass holiday, a genuine holiday of the people.” His was an attempt to document Soviet daily life as qualitatively different from that of previous times, changed by the revolution, commensurate with the Stalinist claim to have revolutionized everyday life.

认为日记应该是历史导向的才能成为合法的个人记录，这种观念反映在日记作者对他们的编年史未能实现这种导向的哀叹中。莫斯科共青团员阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫（Anatoly Ulianov）在他的日记第一篇结尾处责备自己“愚蠢地”无法将日记与生活中更有意义的目的联系起来，这份日记在未来的几年里都将围绕着他对一个叫卡佳的女孩不幸的爱而展开：“‘记日记是小资产阶级的’这种说法对吗？我认为，既对也不对。如果你只写爱情，写你在爱情中如何受苦，那大概就是一种肮脏的小资产阶级把戏。”乌里扬诺夫意识到自己有些被这种精神感染了，他发誓要停止练习“废话学”，从此只关注“现实生活”中的“事实”。他指的是“人们写书记录的那种生活”，那些正在建设新社会主义世界的英雄们的生活。相比之下，他的生活（如他的日记所例证的）是空洞的，充斥着沉思，缺乏“存在的本质”。

另一位日记作者、作家亚历山大·佩列古多夫（Alexander Peregudov）直到二十五年后才意识到他的日记项目失败了。在1961年的一篇日记中，他提到在重读30年代的笔记时，他被这些笔记的“琐碎”所震惊：“我们国家发生的那些改变了面貌、增强了实力的伟大事迹都去哪了？我的解释是，这份日记并未注定用于如此崇高的目的，而是用于记录围绕着我的家庭生活和自然的小小的、‘私密且抒情’的笔记，这些笔记只对我自己和玛利亚有很大意义。我现在多么后悔没有写下另一部致力于重大事件的伟大日记。我经常尝试，但我从未写成。”

The sense that a diary should be historical in orientation in order to be a legitimate personal record is reflected in the laments of diarists that their chronicles failed to achieve such an orientation. Concluding the very first entry of his diary, which for years to come would re-volve around his unhappy love for a girl called Katya, the Moscow komsomolist Anatoly Ulianov chided himself for a “stupid” inability to tie his diary to a more significant purpose in life: “Is the saying correct that keeping a diary is petit-bourgeois? Yes and no, I think. If you write only about love, about how you suffer in love, that probably is a foul petit-bourgeois trick.” Realizing that he was somewhat infected by such a spirit, Ulianov vowed to stop practicing “babbology” and henceforth focus only on the “facts” of “real life.” By this he meant “the life people write books about,” the life of the heroes who were building the new socialist world. His life, by contrast, as exemplified by his diary, was empty, filled with brooding thoughts, void of the “essence of existence.”

Another diarist, the writer Alexander Peregudov, realized only from the distance of a quarter-century that his diary project had failed. In an entry of 1961 he related that in rereading his notes from the 1930s he was struck by how “petty” they were: “Where are all the great things that took place in our country, changing its face and strengthening its might? My explanation for this is that the diary was not destined for such a high purpose, but was kept for small, ‘intimate and lyrical’ notes which revolved only around my family life and nature and were of great interest only to myself and Maria. How I regret now that I did not keep a different, a great diary, devoted to the great events. I often tried, but I never wrote it.”

与乌里扬诺夫和佩列古多夫类似，年轻的女教师维拉·帕夫洛娃（Vera Pavlova）遗憾的是她的日记只涉及日常生活中微小而肤浅的插曲，未能触及生活的“宏大而广阔”的问题。她总结道，她的日记太“主观”了，因此“形式上枯燥且模式化”。她告诫自己要“写得更简单些，创造出一些新的东西，让这种新风格揭示、歌颂某个转折点……一个新时期……是的，要写出客观的东西，就必须描绘，必须创造新的形象……浓缩这些事件，用一条线索将它们串联起来，形成一个统一的思想、一种统一的倾向”。从个人观察的角度出发，“主观地”写作生活，不加反思，就是以一种老旧的、缺乏创造力的方式写作。挑战在于把握历史在她个人生活中演进的过程。在1931年和1932年进行这些观察时，帕夫洛娃预示了新兴的社会主义现实主义学说的核心原则，该学说呼吁苏联作家在革命的发展中描绘现实，并将他们的文学角色表现为阶级斗争和迈向无阶级社会进程的浓缩表达。帕夫洛娃揭示了一种独特的叙事期待：要成为一份有价值的记录，她的日记必须致力于时代的指导思想。

Similarly to Ulianov and Peregudov, the young schoolteacher Vera Pavlova regretted that her diary concerned only small and superficial episodes of her daily existence and failed to address the “big and vast” questions of life. Her diary was too “subjective,” she concluded, and hence “boring and schematic in form.” She admonished herself to “write more simply, create something new, so that this new style would reveal, would celebrate some turning-point . . . a new period . . . Yes, to write something objective, one must portray, must create new images . . . to condense the events, and tie them together with a single thread, into a single idea and a single tendency.” To write about life “subjectively,” without reflection, from the standpoint of personal observation, was to write in an old-fashioned, uncreative way. The challenge was to grasp the course of history as it progressed through her personal life. When making these observations in 1931 and 1932, Pavlova prefigured central tenets of the emerging socialist realist doctrine, which called upon Soviet writers to portray reality in its revolutionary development and to present their literary characters as concentrated expressions of the class struggle and the march toward a classless society. Pavlova reveals a distinct narrative expectation: to be a worthwhile record, her diary had to be devoted to the guiding idea of the age.
在将日记构思为历史编年史时，像帕夫洛娃、乌里扬诺夫和维什涅夫斯基这样的日记作者努力将自己塑造为历史主体。日记提供的日历网格帮助他们表达了一种时间意识，而这种意识对于历史主体性的构建至关重要。

来自乌拉尔地区的民族志学家和图书馆馆员弗拉基米尔·比留科夫（Vladimir Biriukov）的日记展示了日历日期如何作为时间标记来区分新时代与旧时代，并将作者牢牢安置在苏维埃领域。比留科夫四十多岁时，批评他母亲为复活节假期做的精心准备，“尽管她非常清楚拉拉（Lara）和我根本不相信复活节之类的东西”。第二天，他评论桌上堆积如山的复活节蛋糕，说剩下的足够用来庆祝五一劳动节了：“让今天的节日成为母亲的节日吧——下一个将是我们的节日。”同样地，列宁格勒工程学教授瓦西里·佩达尼（Vasily Pedani）在1930年孙子斯拉瓦（Slava）出生之际开始写日记。他在1931年4月12日（当时斯拉瓦还不到一岁）记录道，家里教孩子如何回应少先队的问候“准备着！”斯拉瓦“会举起他的小手：‘时刻准备着！’”佩达尼通过指出这一练习发生在传统的复活节假期，强调了他孙子所受教育的共产主义方向。在阅读十九世纪作家伊万·冈察洛夫的小说时，维拉·帕夫洛娃被革命前俄罗斯的生活方式与苏联生活的巨大反差所震撼：“感觉那些事件好像至少发生在几个世纪前……仅仅八十年，却是多么巨大的飞跃——一个历史性的转折。”

In conceiving of their diaries as historical chronicles, diarists like Pavlova, Ulianov, and Vishnevsky were at pains to cast themselves as subjects of history. The calendar grid provided by the diary helped them articulate a temporal consciousness that was central for the formulation of a historical subjectivity.

The diary of Vladimir Biriukov, an ethnographer and librarian from the Ural region, demonstrates how calendar dates could serve as temporal markers to distinguish a new time from an old time and situate the author firmly in the Soviet realm. In his forties, Biriukov criticized his mother’s elaborate preparations for the Easter holiday, “although she knows perfectly well that Lara and I don’t believe in Easter and such things.” The next day he remarked on the mountains of Easter cake on the table, that there would be enough left over to celebrate May Day: “Let today’s holiday be mother’s holiday—the next one will be ours.” In a similar vein, Vasily Pedani, a Leningrad professor of engineering who began to keep a diary in 1930, on the occasion of the birth of his grandson Slava, recorded that on April 12, 1931—when Slava was not yet a year old—the family had taught the child how to respond to the pioneer greeting “Be prepared!” Slava “would raise his little hand: ‘Always prepared!’” By pointing out that this exercise took place on the traditional Easter holiday, Pedani underscored the Communist direction of his grandson’s upbringing. Upon reading a novel by the nineteenth-century writer Ivan Goncharov, Vera Pavlova was struck by how much the lifestyles of pre-revolutionary Russia were at odds with Soviet life: “It seems as if those events took place at least several centuries ago . . . Only eighty years, but what a great leap—a historical turn.”

尼娜·卢戈夫斯卡娅（Nina Lugovskaya，生于1919年）是一位社会革命党老兵的女儿，其父一直受到共产主义当局的骚扰。尽管家里的公寓反复被秘密警察搜查，尼娜的父亲仍督促他的三个女儿记日记，告诉她们当前的时代在晚年回首时将“极其有趣”。尼娜在日记中寻求通过记录周围饥饿和压迫的现实来揭露共产主义宣传的“谎言”。她抱怨自己那些毫无骨气、浑然不觉的同龄人，梦想着过一种革命行动的生活，这在社会革命党的精神下很可能意味着恐怖行为。有一次，她记下了自己打算杀掉斯大林的想法，以报复她父亲所遭受的不公。

列宁格勒历史系学生阿尔卡季·曼科夫（Arkady Mankov）也记了一本日记，里面充满了尖刻的政治评论。和加里宁的档案员朱拉夫廖夫一样，曼科夫将他的日志构思为未来历史学家书写斯大林日常生活史的原始材料，但与朱拉夫廖夫不同，他写日记是为了揭示这个政治体制的不可信。曼科夫写道，苏联当代的社会结构是“纯粹的资本主义”；将其称为马克思主义国家是亵渎神灵的。然而，曼科夫始终呼吁实现马克思的革命目标——结束剥削和实现物质富足。在阐述他的批评时，他强调其进步性质。他把自己描述为一个“革命活动分子”，他“为了未来的理想而反对当代的现实。他知道未来的生活会更好，但只有通过无情地摧毁当前生活的结构才能达到”。

著名的生物化学家弗拉基米尔·维尔纳茨基（Vladimir Vernadsky）在他大清洗时期的日志中，记录了他所在的研究所以及他的朋友和同事中的一波波逮捕潮。维尔纳茨基简洁的记录生动地唤起了清洗运动的狂乱与恐怖。然而，他最强烈的关注点之一是清洗对苏联国家实力的破坏性影响，他断言，这个国家从根本上追求“群众在其全部真实意义上的利益（除了思想自由和宗教自由）”。维尔纳茨基怀疑斯大林及其周围的人陷入了一种集体的精神错乱，否则他们怎么会“毁掉他们引入人类历史的新[秩序]的伟大事业”？这个“伟大事业”就是苏联国家的建设，维尔纳茨基认为，斯大林在这一成就上功不可没。正是这种苏联国家性的理想，促使曾作为自由派立宪民主党领袖和国家主义坚定支持者的维尔纳茨基批判性地审视布尔什维克政权的政策。

Nina Lugovskaya (born in 1919) was the daughter of a Socialist Revolutionary party veteran who kept being harassed by Communist authorities. Despite the fact that the family’s apartment was repeatedly searched by the secret police, Nina’s father urged his three daughters to keep diaries, telling them that the current times would be “exceedingly interesting” to look back on in later years. In her diary Nina sought to expose the “lies” of Communist propaganda by recording the reality of hunger and oppression around her. Complaining about her spineless, oblivious peers, she dreamed of a life of revolutionary action, which in the spirit of the Socialist Revolutionary party could well mean terrorist acts. At one point she jotted down her intention to kill Stalin to avenge the injustices committed against her father.

The Leningrad history student Arkady Mankov also kept a diary that brimmed with acerbic political commentary. Like the Kalinin archivist Zhuravlev, Mankov conceived of his journal as raw material for a history of Stalinist everyday life that historians would write one day, but unlike Zhuravlev, he wrote the diary to discredit the political regime. The contemporary social structure in the Soviet Union, Mankov wrote, was “purely capitalist”; to refer to it as a Marxist state was blasphemous. All the while, however, Mankov called for the realization of Marx’s revolutionary goals—the end of exploitation and the arrival of material plenty. In formulating his critique, he emphasized its progressive quality. He described himself as a “revolutionary activist,” who “opposes contemporary reality . . . in the name of the ideal of the future. He knows that the future life will be better but that it can only be reached by mercilessly destroying the structures of the present life.”

The renowned biochemist Vladimir Vernadsky devoted his journal of the period of the Great Purges to chronicling the waves of arrests at his own research institute and among his friends and colleagues. Vernadsky’s laconic record starkly evokes the frenzy and monstrosity of the purge campaign. Yet one of his strongest concerns was the deleterious effect of the purges on the power of the Soviet state, a state that, he asserted, fundamentally pursued “the interests of the masses in their entire real significance (except for freedom of thought and freedom of religion).” Vernadsky suspected that Stalin and the people surrounding him were gripped by a collective mental disorder, for how else could they “ruin the great cause of the new [order], which they have introduced into the history of mankind”? The “great cause” was the construction of the Soviet state, an accomplishment for which, according to Vernadsky, Stalin deserved personal credit. It was this ideal of Soviet statehood that caused Vernadsky, a former leader of the liberal Kadet party and an ardent proponent of statism, to critically engage the policies of the Bolshevik regime.

尽管代际和职业背景不同，维尔纳茨基和曼科夫对政权的批判视角在结构上惊人地相似。两人都相信将开启完美未来社会秩序的历史发展规律，两人都声称自己在创造未来中发挥着积极作用，且两人都无法理解那些不接受这一愿景而怀念过去的人。其中就有曼科夫的叔叔，一位被剥夺选举权的前商人。曼科夫斥责他的叔叔——一个表面上“和蔼”的人——持有一种消极和倒退的态度：“万尼亚叔叔是一个普通平庸资产阶级的化身，他对苏联政权、对一切现实事物充满了卑鄙的仇恨，这种人连同收入一起被剥夺了所有的存在目的和生活的理由。”以同样的果决，作家米哈伊尔·普里什文（Mikhail Prishvin）反对重回过去的可能：“东正教十字架……君主制……神父……追思弥撒……乡村巡警……土地长官——不可能！”尽管普里什文谴责苏联国家非人道的政策，他仍将这个时代构思为一个历史必然的铁器时代，要求其公民遵守纪律和顺从。他的每日日记用于记录“历史之风”的律动。

Notwithstanding their different generational and occupational backgrounds, Vernadsky’s and Mankov’s critical perspectives on the regime were strikingly similar in structure. Both men believed in laws of historical development that would usher in a perfect future social order, both claimed for themselves an active role in the creation of the future, and neither could understand people who did not accept this vision and instead looked to the past. Among those was Mankov’s uncle, a disenfranchised former merchant. Mankov castigated his uncle, an outwardly “pleasant” man, for having a negative and retrograde attitude: “Uncle Vanya is an embodiment of vile hatred toward Soviet power, toward everything that is real, on the part of an average philistine-bourgeois who, along with his income, has been deprived of all purpose for existence and every reason to live.” With the same resoluteness, the writer Mikhail Prishvin opposed a possible return to the past: “The Orthodox cross . . . the monarchy . . . priests . . . funeral masses . . . village constables . . . land captains—impossible!” Even though Prishvin condemned the inhumane policies of the Soviet state, he conceived of the era as a historically necessary iron age that demanded discipline and compliance on the part of its citizens. His daily diary served to record the movements of the “wind of history.”

无论政治立场如何，这些日记作者都流露出一种强烈的意识，即他们的时代是一个历史时代，而他们自己是有义务参与创造社会主义世界的历史主体。在这一大批日记中，有几份由于避开了革命的意义地平线而脱颖而出。其中包括叶夫多基姆·尼古拉耶夫（Evdokim Nikolaev）的日记，他是一位出生于1872年的自学成才的莫斯科工人，曾是立宪民主党成员。1920年，尼古拉耶夫因涉嫌反革命活动被捕，他拥有约一万册藏书的私人图书馆随后被没收。在经历了一系列进一步的逮捕后，他于1938年被处决。在整个苏联时期，尼古拉耶夫在日记中严格遵守旧的儒略历（比1918年引入的格里高利历晚十三天）。他虔诚地用革命前的名字称呼当地的街道和工厂。与贬低复活节而援引五一节的民族志学家比留科夫相反，苏联的劳动节反而触动尼古拉耶夫怀念起沙皇统治下的生活：“那时候大家觉得多么愉快和快乐。万物是多么丰盈，一切又是多么便宜和幸福……这一切都像梦一样消失了。一场动乱发生了，那些对这个国家和俄罗斯人民来说是异己的罪犯从流放地回来了。他们篡夺了对俄罗斯人民的权力，开始进行一个接一个的实验。”与其他以更好的未来之名谴责当前政权的批评者不同，尼古拉耶夫谴责革命事业本身，认为它是“某种为人民安排集体农庄生活的乌托邦式、毫无意义的制度，这个制度完全通过胁迫和恐怖来运行”。

伊格纳特·弗罗洛夫（Ignat Frolov）是来自莫斯科地区的集体农庄农民，他在斯大林时代的日记中也遵循儒略历。然而，他并没有将日记用于政治目的。他的记录演变成了一份自然季节的循环历法，配有对天气和马铃薯作物状况的详细日常观察。他提到了所有的俄罗斯宗教节日。只是偶尔，叙述流会被关于管理集体农庄的“无神论”共产党人恶行的言论所打断。弗罗洛夫的日记没有任何自我反思或内省的迹象，它是前现代意识的一个典型案例——生活在受自然力量和宗教支配的宇宙中。

相比于那些热切要求参与革命时代的日记，后一类日记显然属于少数。这不仅仅是因为保留这种异议日记存在危险，导致数量较少；卢戈夫斯卡娅、曼科夫和普里什文的日记在政治上至少同样具有爆炸性。问题在于，把自己排除在革命时间之外会带来自我边缘化。在一个政治动员和公众参与的时代，很难“保持沉默……只是站在场边”，就像另一位来自乌拉尔地区、有着“反革命”政治记录的农民安德烈·阿尔日洛夫斯基（Andrei Arzhilovsky）描述自己的困境那样。
许多苏联日记作者发现，拥护声名狼藉的沙皇政权作为共产主义国家的替代品甚至更不可取，而这恰恰是叶夫多基姆·尼古拉耶夫对苏联政权的彻底否定所导致的方向。

Whatever their political differences, these diarists all bespoke an intense consciousness of their time as a historical age and of themselves as historical subjects with a duty to participate in the creation of the socialist world. Against this corpus of diaries, several others stand out that eschew the revolutionary horizon of meaning. Among them is the diary of Evdokim Nikolaev, a self-educated Moscow worker born in 1872 and a former member of the Kadet party. Nikolaev’s private library, numbering some ten thousand books, was confiscated following his arrest in 1920 for alleged counterrevolutionary activities. After a series of further arrests, he was executed in 1938. Throughout the Soviet period, in his diary, Nikolaev strictly observed the old Julian calendar, which lagged behind the Gregorian calendar, introduced in 1918, by thirteen days. He referred religiously to local streets and factories by their prerevolutionary names. In contrast to the ethnographer Biriukov, who denigrated Easter to invoke May Day, Nikolaev was moved by the Soviet labor holiday to reminisce about life under tsarism: “How merry and joyful everybody felt back then. What a wealth of everything existed, and how inexpensive and happy everything was . . . All this has vanished, like a dream. A disturbance occurred, and criminal people, alien to the country and the Russian people, came back from exile. They seized power over the Russian people and began to perform one experiment after another.” Unlike other critics who condemned the current regime in the name of a better future, Nikolaev denounced the revolutionary enterprise as such as a “utopian and senseless system of some sort of a kolkhoz life for the people, a system that operates solely through coercion and terror.”

Ignat Frolov, a kolkhoz peasant from the Moscow region, also observed the Julian calendar in his Stalin-era diary. He, however, did not use his diary for political ends. His record evolved as a cyclical calendar of the natural seasons, complete with detailed daily observations on the weather and the state of the potato crop. He mentioned all the Russian religious holidays. Only occasionally was the narrative flow punctuated by remarks on the pernicious deeds of the “godless” Communists who ran the kolkhoz. Frolov’s diary showed no sign of self-reflection or introspection, and it is an exemplary case of premodern consciousness—life in a universe governed by the forces of nature and religion.

There were notably fewer of these last-mentioned diaries than of those clamoring for involvement in the revolutionary age. It was not just the danger of keeping such a dissenting journal that kept the numbers low; Lugovskaya’s, Mankov’s, and Prishvin’s diaries were at least as politically explosive. At issue, rather, was the self-marginalization that ensued from writing oneself out of revolutionary time. In an age of political mobilization and public participation it was difficult to “keep quiet . . . and just stand on the sidelines,” as another diarist, Andrei Arzhilovsky, a peasant from the Ural region with a “counterrevolutionary” political record, described his plight.

Many Soviet diarists found it even less desirable to endorse the discredited tsarist regime as an alternative to the Communist state, and yet this was precisely the direction in which Evdokim Nikolaev’s total rejection of the Soviet regime led him.

作家普里什文意识到了共产主义时代自我边缘化的问题。在评论知识分子与布尔什维克党之间关系的历史时（他将其解释为以文化换取政治行动主义），他总结道：“尽管[布尔什维克]认为他们在掌权，但我们认为最终我们会领导他们。与此同时，那些留在场边的人变成了老处女。”娜杰日达·曼德尔施塔姆记载说，她的哥哥叶夫根尼常说，苏联政权对知识分子所掌握的大部分权力都承载在“革命”这个词上，“[知识分子的任何成员]都无法忍受放弃它。一个又一个民族都屈服于这个词，它的力量如此之大，以至于人们不禁要问，为什么我们的统治者还需要监狱和死刑。”曼德尔施塔姆补充说，“革命”的诱惑甚至占据了她同时代人中“最值得尊敬”的人，包括她自己的丈夫奥西普。普里什文和娜杰日达·曼德尔施塔姆只提到了党和知识分子，但正如大量来自下层阶级的自学成才的日记作者所显示的那样，投身革命的召唤远远超出了这两个群体。

The writer Prishvin recognized the problem of self-marginalization in the Communist age. Commenting on the history of the relationship between the intelligentsia and the Bolshevik party, which he in-terpreted as a trade of culture for political activism, he concluded: “Whereas [the Bolsheviks] thought they were in charge, we thought that eventually we would lead them. Meanwhile those who remained on the sidelines turned into spinsters.” Nadezhda Mandelstam reported that her brother Evgeny used to say that much of the power wielded by the Soviet regime over the intelligentsia was carried in the word “Revolution,” “which [no member of the intelligentsia] could bear to give up. It is a word to which whole nations have succumbed, and its force was such that one wonders why our rulers still needed prisons and capital punishment.” Mandelstam added that the allure of “the Revolution” had taken hold of even the “most worthy” of her contemporaries, including her own husband Osip. Prishvin and Nadezhda Mandelstam addressed only the party and the intelligentsia, but as the great number of self-educated diarists from the lower classes suggests, the appeal to get involved in the revolution extended far beyond these two groups.

20世纪30年代中期的两本日记说明了激发如此多自我反思日记记录的历史意识的程度和局限。虽然两者都是由归国侨民撰写的，但它们在基调和导向上却截然不同。尼古拉·乌斯特里亚洛夫是一位法学教授，曾是白卫军军官，内战后移居中国，他长期以来一直羡慕苏联革命事业的“历史激情”。他于1935年回到苏联，渴望投身于新世界的建设。乌斯特里亚洛夫用他的日记记录了他在莫斯科到处看到的历史黎明的迹象。年轻运动员列队走过红场的景象加强了他的信念，即“我们的革命”是“一次高涨、一个开端、一个新的辩证周期中的正题”。在他的观察中有一种强烈的自我反思成分，因为他相信只有通过他洞察历史运作的能力，他才能“赢得一份苏联传记”。乌斯特里亚洛夫知道，他作为前白卫军军官的记录将使他难以在新秩序中占据一席之地。此外，列队行进的年轻运动员的景象增强了他感到自己已老去、被历史抛弃的感觉。但他无法想象在历史走向完成的过程中仅仅做一个旁观者：“在这些日子里，当似乎每个人都发现自己有那么多事情要做时，很难觉得自己是一个‘多余的人’。我希望全身心地投入到活动中——只要不在我们这个时代、在这个历史时刻成为多余的人——当我们的伟大国家、我们的伟大革命的命运正在被决定时。你希望在苏联人民、苏联爱国者中充分保持自己的地位，而你痛苦地忍受着令人厌恶的孤立，以及四面八方包围着你的冷酷‘警惕’和威严的不信任。”乌斯特里亚洛夫于1937年夏天因阴谋罪被捕并被枪杀。

Two diaries of the mid-1930s illustrate the extent and the limits of the historical consciousness that spurred the production of so many self-reflective diaristic records. While both were written by returning émigrés, they could not have differed more in tonality and orientation. Nikolai Ustrialov, a law professor and one-time officer in the White army who had emigrated to China after the civil war, had long envied the Soviet revolutionary project for its “historical pathos.” He returned to Soviet Russia in 1935, eager to involve himself in the construction of the new world. Ustrialov used his diary to record signs of the historical dawn that he saw breaking everywhere in Moscow. The sight of a youth parade in Red Square reinforced his conviction that “our revolution” was an “upsurge, a beginning, a thesis in a new dialectical cycle.” There was a strong self-reflexive component in his observations, for he believed that only through his ability to see the work of history could he “earn a Soviet biography.” Ustrialov knew that his record as a former White officer would make it difficult for him to claim a place in the new order. Moreover, the sight of the parading young athletes reinforced his sense of being old and outlived by history. But he could not conceive of being a mere bystander as history marched toward completion: “It is difficult to feel like a ‘superfluous person’ these days, when, it would seem, everyone finds themselves with so much to do. I want to be up to my neck in activity—if only not to be superfluous in our time, at this historic hour—when the fate of our great country, our great revolution, is being decided. You want to hold your own to the fullest extent among the Soviet people, Soviet patriots, and you painfully endure your hateful isolation and the stares of cold ‘vigilance’ and dignified distrust that surround you on all sides.” Ustrialov was arrested on conspiracy charges in the summer of 1937 and shot.

另一位归国侨民是塔季扬娜·列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜，她是一位歌手和诗人，曾在西欧和美国生活，在与美国丈夫离婚后于1935年回到莫斯科。列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜既没有采纳也没有拒绝苏联革命的自我转型特质。与20世纪30年代的许多苏联移民（其中包括数十名逃离纳粹德国的德国共产党员）不同，她没有提到她回到俄罗斯的任何政治原因。吸引她回来的是压倒性的乡愁。由于以前没有接触过苏联体制，她不习惯对日常生活进行政治解读；她的观察是由一种在当时许多其他日记中缺失的审美感受力所塑造的。她描述了自己对公共场所人际交往粗鲁的震惊，对“挤满了打架、叫喊、互相侮辱且气味难闻的人的电车”感到惊骇。她带着年幼的女儿去动物园，一个坐在她旁边长椅上的男人盯着她看。当她对他微笑时，他开口了：“请原谅我，就在最近我去了特列季亚科夫美术馆。你就像我在那里看到的一位意大利圣母。我还没见过这样的女人。让人无法移开视线。我想一直看着你。”电车上的一个女人也称赞了她的长相：“好了，现在我可以说了：我见过一位美丽的女人。你显然不是俄罗斯人。我从你脸上的表情就能看出你不是我们的人。”

列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜的审美观以个人风格为中心，缺乏时间演进的动态，这与社会主义现实主义审美观截然不同，后者通过对完美未来的瞥见来理解粗糙的现在，并仅通过其社会用途来评估特定的事实。仿佛为了驱散弥漫在莫斯科的那些不快印象，她在日记中唤起了在西班牙度过的三年的回忆：“海洋、悬崖、橘树油亮的绿色、玫瑰和沙子……还有太阳，炫目而壮丽，仿佛整个世界都躺在它下面。它温暖着这整个世界，它在光芒中融化了所有的丑陋、所有的痛苦、所有的疾病。哦，西班牙的太阳——多么幸福！”与许多苏联日记作者相比，列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜在过去的岁月中寻找幸福的源泉，而不是在待建设的灿烂未来中。她将幸福等同于在大自然中平和的生存，而不是在征服自然的积极斗争中。她的立场是沉思的，而非行动主义的。具有讽刺意味的是，她怀旧的段落是献给西班牙的。西班牙在当时苏联的日记中占据显著地位，但大多数日记作者援引的是一种截然不同的西班牙形象——一个正在进行英勇内战、抗击法西斯势力的国家。西班牙并非作为金色往昔记忆的投射载体，而是被表现为激烈的阶级斗争的舞台，未来的命运在那里被决定。

事实上，列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜对西班牙的想法在写下这篇日记后的几周内发生了重大演变。在报纸上读到法西斯对她所珍爱的西班牙城市的轰炸袭击后，她意识到她的记忆所具有的“样板化”特质与丑恶的战争现实之间的张力。她接受了向雕塑家和艺术家联盟发表关于西班牙演讲的邀请，并对她的演讲所引起的狂热反响感到高兴和惊讶。随后，这篇演讲发表在红军日报《红星报》上。她对西班牙看法的演变表明了苏联宣传意象不仅塑造个人自我定义、甚至塑造其记忆的力量。1947年，在战后初期的排外气候中，列什琴科-苏霍姆利娜被捕并被判处八年劳改。

The other returning emigrant was Tatiana LeshchenkoSukhomlina, a singer and poet who had lived in Western Europe and the United States and returned to Moscow in 1935 after divorcing her American husband. Leshchenko-Sukhomlina neither took up nor rejected the self-transformative ethos of the Soviet revolution. Unlike many Soviet immigrants of the 1930s, among them scores of German Communists who had escaped from Nazi Germany, she cited no political reasons for her return to Russia. What drew her back was an overwhelming homesickness. With no previous exposure to the Soviet system, she was not conditioned to subject daily life to a political reading; her observations were shaped by an aesthetic sensibility absent in many other diaries of the period. She described her shock at the coarseness of human encounters in public, at the “streetcar, which is packed with people who fight and shout, who insult each other and smell bad.” At the zoo, where she went with her young daughter, a man sitting on a bench next to her stared at her. When she smiled at him he spoke: “Forgive me, just recently I was at the Tretyakov Gallery. You are like an Italian Madonna I saw there. I haven’t seen any woman like this. It’s impossible to tear oneself away. I want to look at you all the time.” A woman on the streetcar also praised her looks: “Well, now I can say I have seen a beautiful woman. You are obviously not Russian. I can tell from the expression on your face that you’re not one of us.”

Leshchenko-Sukhomlina’s aesthetics, centering on individual style and lacking any temporal dynamic, differed starkly from socialist realist aesthetics, which apprehended the coarse present through glimpses of the perfect future and evaluated a given fact only through its social use. As if to banish the unpleasant impressions engulfing her in Moscow, she evoked in her diary memories of three years she had spent in Spain: “the ocean, the cliffs, the glossy green of the orange trees, the roses and the sand . . . And the sun, blinding and magnificent, as if the whole world were lying below it. And it warms this entire world, it melts in its rays all ugliness, all bitterness, all disease. Oh, sun of Spain—what happiness!” In contrast to many Soviet diarists, Leshchenko-Sukhomlina found the source of her happiness in a bygone past, not in a radiant future to be constructed. She equated happiness with a peaceful existence in nature, not in an active struggle to subjugate nature. Her stance was contemplative, not activist. It is ironic that her nostalgic passage is devoted to Spain. Spain figured prominently in Soviet diaries of the period, but most diarists invoked a very different image of Spain—a nation engaged in a heroic civil war against the forces of fascism. Rather than serving as a projection for memories of a golden past, Spain was represented as an arena of bitter class struggle, in which the future was being decided.

In fact, Leshchenko-Sukhomlina’s thinking about Spain evolved significantly in the weeks following this diary entry. After reading in the newspapers about the fascist bombing raids on Spanish cities that were dear to her, she recognized a tension between the “stenciled” quality of her memories and the ugly reality of war. She accepted an invitation to give a speech on Spain to the Union of Sculptors and Artists and was pleased and amazed by the enthusiastic response to her presentation. It was subsequently published in the Red Army daily, Krasnaya zvezda. The evolution of her notions of Spain suggests the power of Soviet propagandistic imagery to shape not only individuals’ self-definition but even their memories. In 1947, amid the xenophobic climate of the immediate postwar period, Leshchenko-Sukhomlina would be arrested and sentenced to eight years in a forced-labor camp.

zh: 自我转型的功夫
en: The Work of Self-Transformation

children: 使自我与历史保持一致需要付出努力和斗争。日记记录了这一过程，同时也帮助实现了这一过程。20世纪30年代的许多日记允许日记作者观察自己的生理与智力活动，目的是控制和完善它们。为了记录他们的自我转型工作，日记作者反复援引“计划”、“斗争”和“意识”等概念，这些是最初几个五年计划时期共产主义的核心价值观。

It took work and struggle to align the self with history. Diaries documented this process as much as they helped bring it about. Many diaries from the 1930s allowed the diarists to monitor their own physiological and intellectual processes for the purpose of controlling and perfecting them. To document their self-transformative work, diarists repeatedly invoked the concepts of “planning,” “struggle,” and “consciousness,” core Communist values of the period of the first Five-Year Plans.

年轻的女教师维拉·帕夫洛娃指出，她将个人生活划分为五年计划，其日期与苏联政府制定的官方五年计划相对应。她为“自我”勾勒的建设目标，以及她对生产配额达成和超额达成的自豪陈述（“在这一战线上，五年计划已在两年半内完成”），说明了帕夫洛娃的假设，即她的个人生活必须作为社会主义建设更广泛的总计划的一部分而发展。她反复表达了控制和理顺生活的需要，希望揭示她“潜意识感受”的领域。她还在日记中倾诉了她的梦想和幻想，以及她所有的“疯狂”想法，但最重要的是将印象“系统化”的愿望，并最终以“计划性的”、“系统性的”方式生活。

The young schoolteacher Vera Pavlova noted that she had divided her personal life into five-year plans, the dates of which corresponded to the official five-year plans established by the Soviet state. The construction targets she outlined for “my self,” as well as her proud statements of production quotas met and exceeded (“on this front the FiveYear Plan has been met in two and a half years”), illustrate Pavlova’s assumption that her personal life had to develop as part and parcel of the wider general plan of socialist construction. Repeatedly she voiced the need to control and rationalize her life, hoping to bring to light the realm of her “subconscious feelings.” She also confided to the diary her dreams and fantasies, all her “crazy” thoughts, but above all a desire to “systematize” impressions and, ultimately, to live her life in “planlike,” “systematic” fashion.

像帕夫洛娃一样，莫斯科工人和共青团积极分子阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫援引“计划”作为一种结构，为他的生活带来秩序并提高工作表现：“我想把工作的计划性传递到我的日常生活中，无论是脑力体力[活动]还是闲暇。我会尝试通过这种方式使我的工作更易于管理。少来些惯常的把戏（与‘诡诈的’卡佳散步等）。”乌里扬诺夫决心对抗亲密关系的纠缠：“我必须把自己置于真实的轨道上，把自己转向理性的头脑、正确的精神活动、一个系统。”作家维拉·因贝尔主张所谓的“‘灵魂技术化’……换句话说，建构主义”，以对抗她在日记中反复诊断出的“灵魂中的混乱”。与这一机械意象相呼应，她在别处写道：“人是一个工厂。而思想是这个工厂的厂长。”无论是否有意，因贝尔都呼应了列宁的话，列宁曾将共产党形容为一个工厂，而中央委员会就是其厂长。

Like Pavlova, the Moscow worker and Komsomol activist Anatoly Ulianov invoked the plan as a structure to bring order to his life and increase his work performance: “I want to transmit the planning of work to my daily life, both for my mental-physical [activities] and for leisure. I will try to make my work more manageable this way. Fewer of the usual tricks (walks with the ‘perfidious’ Katya, etc.).” Ulianov resolved to fight the entanglements of intimate relationships: “I must position myself on real rails, switch myself toward a rational mind, correct mental activity, a system.” The writer Vera Inber advocated what she called “‘technicizing the soul’ . . . in other words, constructivism,” to fight the “disorder in my soul” that she repeatedly diagnosed in her diary. In keeping with this mechanical imagery she remarked elsewhere: “Man is a factory. And the mind is the director of this factory.” Consciously or not, Imber echoed Lenin, who had described the Communist party as a factory, with the Central Committee as its director.

日记作者建立了各种相关的二分法来描述自我的构成以及他们认为自己参与其中的自我转型机制。这些二元对立包括头脑与身体、日记作者的“意志”与他的“心”、或者个人的“意识形态”与他们的“心理”之间的对立。煤矿工人弗拉基米尔·莫洛多佐夫描述了最后一种对立：“有趣的是，心理和意识形态之间有多大的差距。在意识形态上，我动员自己去弥合这一差距，我确实在积极工作，但心理仍然把我拉回家，拉回到我的家庭环境。这两天更频繁的梦境证明了这一点，在梦里我见到了母亲。但意识形态会改善心理，这一定会发生。”
在苏联早期的日记中，“心理”一词总是带有负面色彩。它是一种卑微、混乱且危险的力量，运作在精神和肉体的阴暗角落，日记作者偶尔会承认自己内心潜伏着这种力量。相比之下，意识形态是通过一个人反对心理的自觉斗争而获得的。在个人层面上，它代表了对历史和社会发展规律的更高知识领域的某种主观洞察，这种洞察在制度上被共产党所主张，并具有相同的名称：意识形态。

Diarists established a variety of related dichotomies to describe the composition of their self and the mechanisms of self-transformation in which they saw themselves engaged. These binaries included the opposition between the mind and the body, a diarist’s “will” and his “heart,” or individuals’ “ideology” and their “psychology.” Vladimir Molodtsov, a coal miner, described this last opposition: “It’s interesting how much disparity there is between psychology and ideology. Ideologically, I mobilized myself to bridge the gap, and I do work actively, but the psychology still draws me back home, to my home environment. This is evidenced by the more frequent dreams of the past two days, in which I saw my mother. But ideology will improve psychology, this must happen.”

“Psychology,” in diaries of the early Soviet period, invariably had a negative ring. It was a lowly, chaotic, and dangerous force operating in the dark recesses of spirit and body, a force that diarists occasionally admitted to harboring in themselves. Ideology, by contrast, was attained through a person’s conscious struggle against psychology. On the individual level it represented a subjective insight into a realm of higher knowledge of the laws of historical and social development, an insight that was institutionally claimed by the Communist party and bore the same name, ideology.
斯捷潘·波德卢布内是一个被“我的心理问题”折磨的富农之子，他认为自己从父亲那里继承了根深蒂固的富农心理，无法逃脱。出身于非共产党知识分子的维拉·因贝尔暗示她内心有一种“小资产阶级的混乱”，威胁要吞没她新获得的理性世界观。心理只有依靠理性的头脑和意志的共同力量才能被有效掌控。这两股力量组织了个人的心理-生理机制。一旦它们使心理变得透明和理性，它就不再是心理，而是升华到了纯粹意识形态的层面。

由于“心理”具有反苏含义，日记作者更愿意承认他人受到“心理”的支配，而非承认自己也如此。在与一位承认被高薪吸引而从事采矿工作的农民出身的同事谈话后，莫洛多佐夫愤慨地评论了那个人的“农民心理”：“只看到他的个人利益，只相信他自己。”维拉·帕夫洛娃在阅读了一篇关于瑞典“火柴大王”伊瓦尔·克鲁格自杀的新闻报道后，反思了“当代资产阶级的心理”——这种心理预示着当前西方盛行的“物质和精神危机”。她的推理建立了从“心理”到精神崩溃再到自杀的逻辑进程。

Stepan Podlubny, a kulak’s son tormented by the “question of my psychology,” assumed that he had inherited an ingrained kulak psyche from his father and would be unable to escape it. Vera Inber, hailing from the non-Communist intelligentsia, alluded to a “petit-bourgeois disorder” inside her that threatened to engulf her newly acquired rational worldview. Psychology could effectively be mastered only with the joint powers of the rational mind and the will. These two forces organized the individual’s psycho-physical apparatus. As soon as they rendered psychology transparent and rational it ceased to be psychology, rising to the level of pure ideology.

Because of its anti-Soviet connotation, diarists were more generous in recognizing the workings of “psychology” in others than in themselves. Following a conversation with a fellow worker of peasant origins who admitted having been attracted to a coal mining job by its high wage, Molodtsov indignantly commented on the man’s “peasant psychology”: “Sees only his personal gain and believes only in himself.” Vera Pavlova, upon reading a newspaper report about the suicide of the Swedish “match king” Ivar Kreuger, reflected on the “psychology of the contemporary bourgeoisie”—a psychology indicative of the “material and spiritual crisis” currently reigning in the West. Her reasoning established a logical progression from “psychology” to spiritual breakdown to suicide.

“心理”也是日记作者眼中造成他们在20世纪30年代期间了解到的许多反苏罪行的因素。沃罗涅日省的一位教师齐娜伊达·德尼谢夫斯卡娅在报纸上读到该省存在一个有害的“劳动农民党”，涉及她的几位熟人时感到困惑：“我不明白这一切……他们的心理对我来说完全陌生。他们是谁——傻瓜、疯子，还是混蛋？”老孟什维克列夫·戴奇将他在报纸上读到的右派-托洛茨基主义力量的新阴谋描述为一场“噩梦”，并感到无法“理解这些人的心理，是什么驱使了他们，以及他们寄希望于什么”。在1937年的政治清洗中，剧作家弗谢沃洛德·维什涅夫斯基在日记中记下了关于“敌人及其代理人……叛徒的心理……可能源于他们对人民、对党的力量的不信任……这些是精神上的失败主义者，恶毒且渺小……面对资本的投降者……我正在读关于列宁的书，他的顽强，他的意志。”

正如维什涅夫斯基和帕夫洛娃的日记所显示的，如果不积极加以应对，心理在精神上就是软弱、失败主义的。相比之下，意识则为个人提供了目标感，从而增强了他们的意志力，依靠这种力量，他们要根据自己的自觉设计来重塑世界和自己。没有哪位布尔什维克领导人比列宁拥有更多的意志力，他是所有布尔什维克领导人中意识最高的一位。通过研究列宁的一生，维什涅夫斯基试图为自己汲取列宁钢铁意志的一部分，从而抵御那无形却无处不在的反革命阴谋。

“Psychology” was also what diarists saw as the factor responsible for the many anti-Soviet crimes of which they learned in the course of the 1930s. Zinaida Denisevskaya, a teacher in Voronezh province, was bewildered when she read in the newspapers of a pernicious “Toiling Peasant party” in the province, which involved several of her acquaintances: “I don’t understand all of this . . . Their psychology is completely alien to me. Who are they—fools, psychopaths, or bastards?” Lev Deich, an Old Menshevik, described the new conspiracy of Rightist-Trotskyist forces about which he read in the newspapers as a “nightmare” and felt unable to “understand the psychology of these people, what motivated them, and what they were banking on.” In the midst of the political purges of 1937 the playwright Vsevolod Vishnevsky jotted down in his diary thoughts about “the enemies and their agents . . . the psychology of the traitors . . . Probably from their distrust in the strength of the people, the party . . . These are spiritual defeatists, spiteful and petty . . . Capitulators in the face of capital . . . I’m reading about Lenin, his stubbornness, his will.”

If not actively engaged, psychology was weak and defeatist in spirit—as indicated in the diaries of Vishnevsky and Pavlova. Consciousness, by contrast, supplied individuals with a sense of purpose and thereby increased their willpower, on the strength of which they were to remake the world and themselves according to their conscious designs. Nobody possessed as much willpower as Lenin, the most conscious of all Bolshevik leaders. In studying Lenin’s life, Vishnevsky sought to appropriate for himself a part of Lenin’s iron will and thereby shield himself against the invisible but ubiquitous workings of counterrevolutionary conspiracy.

日记作者将意志描述为与个人的主体性同延。它是在疏导一个人无组织的心理-生理力量的工作中提炼出来的。一旦被激活，它就是一种自主的力量，将自我提升到历史行动者的层面。日记担负着塑造和加强作者意志的关键任务。阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫在日记中诊断自己性格中的坏特质（包括他不受控制的天性和反复无常）时，将这些归因于他意志薄弱：“意志力……它在一个人的身上出现应该始终能保证他过上良好的、有意识的生活。我没有这种意志。这就是为什么（通过批评的方式）我意志薄弱、坐立不安、轻浮且匆忙。我的紧张感和暴躁脾气每次都让我心烦意乱。是的，意志就是一切。”乌里扬诺夫向往的理想是“洁净的、数学化的生活”，这要通过“意志力和政治饱和”来实现。为了实现这个目标，他决心：“具体来说，我为自己设定的任务是，从1933年1月1日到3月1日，至少学习六卷本的列宁选集，对其进行思考，并与你[日记]分享我的见解以及在阅读过程中可能出现的所有不清楚的问题。”

Diarists described the will as coterminous with a person’s subjectivity. It was distilled in the work of channeling a person’s unorganized psycho-physical forces. Once activated, it was an autonomous power that raised the self to the level of a historical agent. The diary had the crucial task of shaping and strengthening its author’s will. While diagnosing in his diary the bad traits in his personality (which included his uncontrolled nature and inconstancy), Anatoly Ulianov attributed these to his weak will: “Willpower . . . its presence in a person should always guarantee him a good, conscious life. I don’t have this will. This is why (by way of criticism) I am weak-willed, restless, frivolous, and hasty. My nervousness and my quick-tempered character unsettle me every time. Yes, the will is everything.” The ideal to which Ulianov aspired was a “clean, mathematical life,” to be attained through “willpower and political saturation.” To realize this goal, he resolved: “Concretely, I am setting myself the task, for the period from January 1 to March 1, 1933, to study at least the six-volume Lenin edition, to ponder over it, and to share with you [the diary] my opinions and all the un-clear questions that may arise during the reading.”

煤矿工人弗拉基米尔·莫洛多佐夫曾将梦中出现的母亲视为他落后心理的证据，他在随后的日记条目中纠正了自己：“当我写到意志与‘心’之间的矛盾时，我有些不正确。只有当一个人的脑子里充斥着‘面包’、‘吃饭’、‘起床’和‘睡觉’时，才会感觉到这种矛盾。在下面的矿井里没有‘矛盾’；只有统一和完整——生产、煤炭、装满更多的货车。”一旦个体工人进入工作领域，他的身体和心理就会经历双重转化：它们被集体化，汇入劳动集体整体的身体和情感；又被组织起来，进入五年计划的图表。莫洛多佐夫将这一过程体验为他理性意志的展开。由于意志的胜利，他毫不费力地工作，带着最高的奉献精神和明确的目标：“我在短暂的一生中能体验到的最高情感，就是意识到我是矿工集体的一部分。”

Vladimir Molodtsov, the coal miner who had taken the appearance of his mother in his dreams as evidence of his backward psychology, corrected himself in a subsequent diary entry: “I was somewhat incorrect when I was writing about the contradiction between the will and the ‘heart.’ This contradiction is felt only when in one’s head there is ‘bread,’ ‘meals,’ ‘get up,’ and ‘go to sleep.’ Down below in the mine there are no ‘contradictions’; there is only unity and wholeness—production, coal, fill more wagons.” As soon as the individual worker entered the work sphere, his body and psyche underwent a double transformation: they were collectivized, in joining the body and the feelings of the laboring collective as a whole; and they were organized, in entering the charts and graphs of the Five-Year Plan. Molodtsov experienced this process as the unfolding of his rational will. Thanks to its triumph he worked effortlessly, with highest devotion and clarity of purpose: “The highest feeling that I could experience in my short life is the feeling of being conscious of the fact that I am a part of the miners’ collective.”

斯捷潘·波德卢布内用道德理想来描述意志力：“长期以来，我一直喜欢意志坚强的人。不管这个人是谁，如果他有强大的意志力，他就是一个好人。”波德卢布内刻苦地记录了他感到自己意志力增强的时刻，但与莫洛多佐夫不同，他的日记在很大程度上是一份失败记录。在总结自己在工作和生活中的总体表现时，他曾得出结论：“我缺乏控制自己的意志力。在目前这一时刻，我有一种巨大的、庞大的、可怕的意志无能。这是所有不幸的源头，也是我的主要缺点。一个最可怕、最危险的缺点，可能对生命造成危险。因为一切都取决于它。”然而，日记不仅仅是关于意志“病态”的公报。写作也是一种治疗；波德卢布内推理说，通过强迫自己定期写作，他也会增强自己的意志力。

Stepan Podlubny described willpower in terms of a moral ideal: “For a long time, I have liked people with a strong will. No matter who this person is, if he has great willpower he is a good person.” Podlubny assiduously recorded instances when he felt that his own willpower had increased, but unlike Molodtsov’s, his diary was for the most part a record of his failures. Summarizing his performance at work and in life in general, he once concluded: “I lack the willpower to control myself. At the present moment I have a big, enormous, terrible impotence of the will. This is the source of all misfortunes and is my main shortcoming. A most dreadful, most dangerous shortcoming that can prove dangerous to life. Because everything depends on it.” Yet the diary was more than a bulletin of a “sick” will. Writing was also a cure; Podlubny reasoned that by forcing himself to write regularly he would also increase his willpower.

意志力是通过斗争获得的。20世纪30年代的日记中充斥着将生活视为持续斗争的表述。莫洛多佐夫日记中的一个条目写道：“现在大家都睡着了……好小伙子们！……荣耀和荣誉属于他们。活着而斗争，是多么美好；斗争着而活着，也是如此。”农村党的积极分子亚历山大·热列兹尼亚科夫描述了他指导的一次干草收割。为了利用一段干燥的天气，他强迫那些反抗的集体农庄农民留在田里直到所有工作完成：“我们一直割到晚上十一点，地割完了。月亮发挥了很大作用，帮助我解决了这个困难的任务。感谢党。它在我身上培养了斗争中的坚定和果敢，以便在最困难的条件下获胜。多么巨大的幸福！……我记得马克思和恩格斯的话：‘斗争就是幸福！’第二天早上又下雨了。”

Willpower was attained through struggle. Diaries of the 1930s abound in references to life as continuous struggle. An entry from Molodtsov’s diary reads: “Everybody is asleep now . . . Splendid lads! . . . Glory and honor to them. How good is it to live, while struggling. And to struggle, while living.” Alexander Zhelezniakov, the rural party activist, described a hay harvest he directed. To take advantage of a spell of dry weather, he coerced the recalcitrant kolkhoz peasants into staying in the field until all work was finished: “We mowed until eleven at night, and the field was mown. The moon played a big role and helped me resolve this difficult task. Thanks to the party. It reared in me firmness and resolve in struggle, to win in the most difficult conditions. What great happiness! . . . I remember the words of Marx and Engels: ‘Struggle is happiness!’ The next morning it rained again.”

工作和斗争是苏联式自我不可或缺的属性；这种自我总被视为一项尚在进行的工程。尼古拉·奥斯特洛夫斯基是一位卧床不起、双目失明的内战老兵，也是自传体小说《钢铁是怎样炼成的》的作者，他向医生解释道：“有些奇怪的人认为，作为一个布尔什维克，可以不每天、每小时都努力训练自己的意志、自己的性格。人必须不断地关注这件事，才不至于滑入小资产阶级的沼泽。真正的布尔什维克不断地锻造和磨练自己。”弗谢沃洛德·维什涅夫斯基似乎在呼应这种劝诫，他遗憾地注意到自己没能做到每天写日记。这阻碍了他实现“更有系统的推进”。在别处，他将自我完善追求中的中断视为停滞甚至退化的时刻。

20世纪30年代的几本日记包含年终总结，有时被称为“结算表”，其明确目的是诊断自我的演变——其成长，或者相反，其停滞或衰退。波德卢布内的日记提供了一个特别引人注目的例子，展示了这种习惯，并表明他是模仿公共领域运作的机制来开展这一实践的：“1933年12月30日整个联盟以及世界各地都在结算年度工作总量。在整个联盟，在许多城市，以及在莫斯科，都在召集会议、大会等，以总结一年的工作。”在评估自己的发展时，波德卢布内选择的词汇几乎与苏联官方结算表的修辞语言完全一致。他的年终日记条目和《真理报》总结年度成就的社论都聚焦于同一个“增长”概念：波德卢布内的个人增长和苏联人口的“迅猛的文化增长”。唯一的差异在于，《真理报》肯定苏联公民中已经发生了“意识的飞跃”，而波德卢布内则抱怨他自己的意识仍然发育不足。

Work and struggle were indispensable attributes of Soviet selfhood, which was always defined as a work in progress. Nikolai Ostrovsky, a bedridden, blinded civil war veteran and author of the autobiographically inspired How the Steel Was Tempered, explained to his doctor: “Some strange people think that it is possible to be a Bolshevik without working every day, every hour on training one’s will, one’s character. One must constantly tend to this matter in order not to slide into the swamp of the petite bourgeoisie. A real Bolshevik constantly forges and polishes himself.” As if echoing this exhortation, Vsevolod Vishnevsky noted with regret that he did not succeed in writing in his diary every day. This prevented him from attaining a “more systematic movement.” Elsewhere he conceived of lapses in his quest for self-perfection as moments of stagnation or even regression.

Several diaries from the 1930s contain end-of-year summaries, sometimes called “balance sheets,” the express purpose of which was to diagnose the evolution of the self—its growth or, alternatively, its stagnation or decline. Podlubny’s diary provides a particularly striking example of this habit, and shows that he modeled the practice on mechanisms operating in the public realm: “12/30/1933 Throughout the entire Union and in countries everywhere they are reckoning up the annual work totals. Throughout the entire Union, in many cities, and in Moscow as well, conferences, congresses, etc., are being convened in order to review the year’s work.” In taking stock of his own development, Podlubny chose terms that were almost completely identical with the rhetorical language of official Soviet balance sheets. His end-of-year diary entry and a Pravda editorial summarizing the year’s achievements both texts focused on the same notion of growth: Podlubny’s personal growth and the “stormy cultural growth” of the Soviet population. The only discrepancy is that where Pravda affirmed that a “leap in consciousness” had taken place among Soviet citizens, Podlubny complained that his own consciousness was still underdeveloped.

zh: 构建或重构自我
en: Constructing or Reconstructing the Self

children: 虽然计划、意识、斗争、心理、意识形态和意志力等概念是那个时代日记的共同属性，但它们源于两种性质不同的自我观念。来自下层阶级（主要是工人和农民）的日记作者努力构建一种他们认为以前并不存在的自我感。与此同时，受教育阶层的成员认为自己拥有一个发育成熟但有问题的自我，需要通过分析和干预来进行转化。只有受教育阶层的成员才能写出维拉·帕夫洛娃（其父亲曾是工厂经理）在日记中所记下的内容：“在过去的几天里，我的‘自我’[moe ‘ia’]经受了（我自己的）详细分析，结合了批评和责备。”

While the concepts of plan, consciousness, struggle, psychology, ideology, and willpower were general attributes of diaries from this age, they proceeded from two qualitatively different notions of self. Diarists from the lower classes, chiefly workers and peasants, labored to construct a sense of self where previously, they believed, none had existed. Members of the educated classes, meanwhile, saw themselves as possessing a developed yet problematic self that required analysis and intervention in order to be transformed. Only a member of the educated classes could write what Vera Pavlova—whose father had been a factory manager–noted in her diary: “During the past days my ‘self’ [moe ‘ia’] was subjected to a detailed analysis (my own), combined with criticism and reproach.”

诚然，每个苏联公民都从旧生活走向新生活。工人和农民也表达了旧的思想行为准则与新准则之间的冲突，但他们很少将自己堕入“旧”习惯（如酗酒、咒骂或虐待配偶）的行为具象化为一个完整的“旧人”形象——即那个必须死去才能让“新人”出现的旧人。他们的习惯是落后的果实，是封建与资本主义制度奴役劳动人民灵魂的结果，这种奴役曾让他们处于近乎非人的生存边缘。像阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫这样的工人将他根深蒂固的粗鲁视为他“动物”般存在的迹象，即内在的野兽。农民出身的工人列昂尼德·波特姆金用物质建设的术语描述了自我改造的需要：他必须在着手建立工厂（即他完成后的自我）之前，先打好地基，搭起框架并围上脚手架。他的重点是自我的“构建”而非“重构”：他并未预见到需要拆除已建立的旧框架或容纳预先存在的建筑部件。

Every Soviet citizen, to be sure, traveled from an old to a new life. Workers and peasants, too, voiced a conflict between old and new codes of thinking and behavior, but they rarely reified their lapses into “old” habits—such as heavy drinking, cursing, or abusing their spouses—into a full-fledged figure of an “Old Man” who had to die in order for the New Man to emerge. Their habits were the fruits of backwardness, results of the feudal-capitalist enslavement of the laboring people’s souls, an enslavement that had kept them on the verge of a subhuman existence. A worker like Anatoly Ulianov regarded his ingrained coarseness as an indication of his “animal”-like existence, the beast within. The peasant-worker Leonid Potemkin described the need to work on his self in terms of material construction: he had to lay a foundation and build a frame surrounded by a scaffolding before he could proceed with setting up the factory, his finished self. His emphasis was on construction, rather than reconstruction, of the self: he did not foresee a need to tear down established old frames or accommodate preexisting building parts.

波特姆金和乌里扬诺夫的叙事轨迹，是从低于人的状态到人的状态，从非人到人。没有哪位日记作者比集体农庄积极分子热列兹尼亚科夫表达得更好了。在期待十月革命十六周年之际，他感叹道：在世界历史上，没有、过去没有、将来也不会有比我们更幸福的一代。我们是新时代的创造者！敌人们，你们这些从四面八方包围着我们的人，你们是否记得，就在二十年前，我们还是微不足道的昆虫，在主人的地板上爬行，而这个曾被资本主义扼杀的渺小的人，在十六年前的11月7日意识到了自己的阶级身份，并将整个世界粉碎到其根基……没有什么比作为一个成员、作为苏联土地的公民并属于列宁那久经沙场考验的共产党更高尚的了……如果十月革命没有发生，我真的能以这种方式理解生活吗，我真的能把自己的个人生活换成对共同目标的斗争吗？不！我本来会一直几乎像动物一样，但现在我很幸福。

叶夫根尼娅·鲁德涅娃（出生于1920年）以女性的口吻表达了同样的想法。1937年11月，她写下这段话时，苏联最高苏维埃第一次选举的准备工作正在进行，这将把纯然苏联的新一代公民引入政治生活，她指出：“我过着充实的生活。我怎能不爱我的祖国，它给了我如此幸福的生活？事实上，如果我出生在革命前，我本来会是什么（是的，正是：什么，而不是谁）？我会成为一个无知的女孩，也许已经是一个新娘，夏天收西红柿，冬天烤面包。”
鲁德涅娃暗示下层女性比其男性同胞受到更严重的压迫；除了作为人的压迫外，她们还被奴役在家庭领域。因此，女性解放包含了人类发展的最大跨度，从尚非人到不受束缚的人。

The trajectory of Potemkin’s and Ulianov’s narratives was from a subhuman to a human state, from non-Man to Man. No diarist expressed this better than the kolkhoz activist Zhelezniakov. In anticipation of the sixteenth anniversary of the October Revolution, he exclaimed: There is not, was not, and will not be, in world history a generation more happy than ours. We are the participants in the creation of a new epoch! Do you recollect, enemies, you who surround us on all sides, that only twenty years ago we were insignificant insects, crawling on the masters’ floors, and this insignificant person, who had been strangled by capitalism, realized himself as a class and shattered the whole world to its foundations on November 7, sixteen years ago . . . There is nothing higher than to be a member, a citizen of the Soviet land and to belong to Lenin’s battle-hardened Communist party . . . Had the October Revolution not taken place, could I really have understood life in this way, and could I really have exchanged my personal life for the struggle for common goals? No! I would have remained almost an animal, but now I am happy.

Evgenia Rudneva (born in 1920) expressed the same thought in a female register. Writing in November 1937, while preparations for the first elections to the USSR’s Supreme Soviet were under way, which was to usher a new generation of purely Soviet citizens into political life, she noted: “I live a full-blooded life. How can I not love my Fatherland, which gives me such a happy life? In fact, what (yes, precisely: what, not who) would I have been, had I been born before the revolution? I would have been an ignorant girl, perhaps already a bride, who would harvest tomatoes in summer and bake bread in winter.”

Rudneva suggested that lower-class women were even more oppressed than their male counterparts; in addition to their oppression as human beings they were enslaved in the domestic sphere. Hence female emancipation comprised the greatest possible span of human development, from not yet human to unfettered humanity.

相比之下，受教育阶层的成员——包括“资产阶级”知识分子的代表以及坚定的共产党员——必须应对他们拥有由革命前文化塑造的有问题的“人格”这一事实。他们以杀死内在的“旧人”并培育“新人”的方式来构想自我转型。不像被没文化的过去所拖累的工农，知识分子成员则苦于文化过剩，需要剥离其非苏联属性。用20世纪20年代转投共产主义的诗人约翰内斯·R·贝彻的话说，知识分子在加入“无产阶级战斗大军”之前，必须“烧掉他从资产阶级族谱中继承的大部分东西……打倒那备受吹捧和神圣化的‘人格’。打倒它那虚假的人为内外举止、它那夸张且矛盾的天性，以及所有刻画‘人格’的反复无常和情绪化的姿态。”当贝彻及其他人贬义地谈论“人格”时，这个词概括了一系列标志着“旧”知识分子的属性：个人主义、自恋、被动、软弱且不适应斗争——一句话，资产阶级的。

By contrast, members of the educated classes—including representatives of the “bourgeois” intelligentsia as well as staunch Communists—had to cope with the fact that they inhabited problematic “personalities” shaped by prerevolutionary culture. They conceived of self-transformation in terms of killing the Old Man and rearing the New Man within. Unlike workers or peasants, who were weighed down by an uncultured past, members of the intelligentsia suffered from an excess of culture which needed to be stripped of its non-Soviet properties. In the words of the poet Johannes R. Becher, who converted to Communism in the 1920s, the intellectual, before joining the “proletarian fighting army,” had to “burn most of what he owes to his bourgeois genealogy . . . Down with the vaunted and sacralized ‘personality.’ Down with its artificial inner and outward comportment, its exaggerated and paradoxical nature, all the capricious and moody posturing characterizing a ‘personality.’” When Becher and others spoke derogatively of “personality,” the term encapsulated a set of attributes marking the “old” intelligentsia: individualistic, narcissistic, passive, soft, and unfit for struggle—in a word, bourgeois.

与其资产阶级本质的斗争是作家尤里·斯列兹金日记中的一个显著主题；事实上，正是这场斗争促使他最初开始写日记。在日记的开篇，46岁的斯列兹金对他三十年的文学职业生涯进行了总结。过去的十年尤其“坎坷和混乱”；因为他的“资产阶级”血统，他既没写出任何重要的东西，也没能出版。这十年被打上了“痛苦的重组需求”和寻找自我的失败尝试的烙印。不过，对于现在和未来，他更有信心：“摆在我面前的是最后一个，同时也是第一个严肃的障碍：摆脱过去，实现现在的自我，克服我所属阶级的惯性。这是一项西绪福斯式的劳作，但我们国家现在必须克服的困难难道不也需要同样的努力吗？因此，一个新的十年，我的第四个十年……愿这本日记成为我的见证者，在创作枯竭的时刻成为我的批评者和激活者。”斯列兹金将阐发新文学风格的职业项目与他克服资产阶级过去的个人追求融合在一起。斯列兹金沉浸在追溯到19世纪中叶的现实主义审美中，他相信为了使他的写作具有合法性和真实性，他必须亲自参与弥漫在整个苏联领域的社会转型议程。他过去的文学作品缺乏实质内容和意义的原因之一，就是他未能参与同内在“旧人”的斗争，从而在本质上保持了资产阶级属性。

另一位具有“资产阶级”背景的作家尤里·奥列沙之所以坚持写日记，也是基于类似的信念，即自传式叙事具有塑造其现实生活的力量。奥列沙转向日记，部分是为了以“事实文学”运动的精神创作文学。他带着几分讽刺，评论了当时流行的新文学时尚，即宣布小说已死，认为只有像日记这样的文献散文才有价值：“愿每个人都写日记：雇员、工人、作家、文化程度不高的人、男人、女人、孩子——这对未来是多么宝贵的财富！”尽管如此，奥列沙还是认真地记日记，不仅是将其作为一种文学实验。他希望对事实记录的追求也能将他那有问题的资产阶级自我牢牢地置于历史轨道上，并带他进入许诺的未来。然而，将纪实技巧应用到奥列沙的个人生活时，却产生了不同的结果。令他懊恼的是，写日记并没有产生转型效果。纪实日记非但没有记录他向新世界的转变，反而记录了他日常生活中“无用”的琐事，从而积累而非消解了他那未改造的旧自我的重量。在撰写和阅读日记的过程中，奥列沙惊恐地发现了初现端倪的“真相”，即他是一个“一生都梦想成为大财产所有者的小资产阶级个人”。

The struggle against his bourgeois essence was a prominent theme in the diary of the writer Yuri Slezkin; in fact, this struggle was what prompted him to keep a diary in the first place. On the opening pages of his journal, Slezkin, aged 46, took stock of the three decades of his literary career. The last decade had been especially “uneven and muddled”; he had neither written anything significant nor been able to publish, because of his “bourgeois” pedigree. The decade had been marked by the “painful need for restructuring” and by unsuccessful attempts to find himself. For the present and future, though, he was more confident: “Before me lies the last, and at the same time the first serious, obstacle: to rid myself of the past, to realize myself in the present, to overcome the inertia of my class. A Sisyphean labor, but doesn’t what our country must now overcome demand the same sort of effort? Thus, a new decade, my fourth decade . . . May this diary be my witness, my critic and activator in the hours of creative exhaustion.” Slezkin conflated the professional project of elaborating a new literary style with his personal quest to overcome his bourgeois past. Steeped in a realist aesthetic reaching back to the mid-nineteenth century, Slezkin believed that for his writing to be legitimate and truthful he had to personally partake in the very agenda of social transformation that pervaded the entire Soviet realm. One reason his past literary work had lacked substance and meaning was that he had failed to engage in the struggle against the former man inside, thus remaining bourgeois in essence.

Yuri Olesha, another writer of “bourgeois” background, was prompted to keep a diary by a similar belief in the power of an autobiographical narrative to shape his actual life. Olesha turned to the diary in part in order to produce literature in the spirit of the “factographic” movement. With a degree of sarcasm, he commented on the new literary fashion of the day, which declared novels to be dead and regarded only documentary prose, such as the diary, as of value: “May everyone write a diary: employees, workers, writers, semi-educated people, men, women, children—what a treasure for the future!” Nevertheless, Olesha pursued his journal in earnest, not only as a literary experiment. He hoped that the pursuit of factography would also place his problematic bourgeois self firmly on a historical track and take him into the promised future. Applied to Olesha’s personal life, however, the techniques of factography produced something else. To his consternation, writing a diary did not have a transformative effect. Instead of documenting his conversion to the new world, the factographic journal recorded the “useless” minutiae of his daily life and thus accumulated, rather than dissipated, the weight of his old, unreformed self. In writing and reading his diary, Olesha discovered with horror the incipient “truth” that he was a “petit-bourgeois individual who all his life has dreamed of becoming a big property-owner.”

奥列沙不仅强迫性地记录他的思想，还记录他的身体症状，焦虑地研究它们可能的含义：它们如何将他定位在历史轨道上？他无法像进步的苏联知识分子那样思考，从而无法使他的主观自我与历史的客观要求保持一致，这最终迫使他承认，他在精神和肉体上都携带着错误的物质。他指出，这个“恐怖的”真相具有生理本质：它“根植在我的血液里，在我大脑的细胞里”。在最糟糕的情况下，奥列沙自我的危机产生了对死亡的恐惧：“我不得不中断写作——去洗个澡……在浴缸里。热——对死亡的恐惧——必须听得更仔细些：是心脏吗？我的大脑出了什么事吗？——没有吗？我经常想到死。有个老头通过看我的笔迹断定我经常想到死。我病态地想到死——太频繁了（几乎是不断地）。”1930年，当奥列沙产生这段关于退化的强烈叙事时（既是他作为个体的退化，也是作为一个社会阶层代表的退化），他只有30岁。然而，生活在对死亡的恐惧中，他无法满怀信心地面对未来。相反，他被拉回到一个他发现无法逃脱的过去。反复翻检过去是奥列沙日记的另一个特征，也是他认为正在塑造他生活以及苏联集体生活的历史项目的一种间接表达。

Olesha obsessively recorded not only his thoughts but also his bodily symptoms, anxiously studying them for possible meaning: How did they situate him on the historical track? His inability to think like a progressive Soviet intellectual, and thus align his subjective self with the objective demands of history, eventually forced him to acknowledge that he carried in himself a wrong substance, spiritual and bodily. This “horrible” truth, he noted, had a physiological essence: it was “ingrained in my blood, in the cells of my brain.” At its worst the crisis of Olesha’s self generated fears of death: “I’ve had to interrupt writing— went to take a bath . . . In the tub. Hot—fear of death—have to listen closer: Is it the heart? Is there something happening to my brain?—isn’t there? I think about death a lot. Some old man determined, by looking at my handwriting, that I think about death a lot. Morbidly, I think about death—too often (almost constantly).” In 1930, when Olesha generated this intense narrative of decline, his decline both as an individual and as a representative of a social class, he was only 30 years old. Yet, living in fear of death, he could not face the future with confidence. Instead he was drawn back into a past from which he found no escape. Recurrent rummaging in the past, another signature of Olesha’s diary, was another mediated expression of the historical project that he believed was shaping his life as well as the life of the Soviet collectivity.

虽然教师维拉·帕夫洛娃与奥列沙有着相同的社会背景（工厂经理的孩子），但她在日记中勾勒出的自我转型叙事却散发出一种总是自我怀疑的奥列沙所不具备的信心和果敢。作为一个对历史唯物主义坚信不疑的人，帕夫洛娃将马克思主义辩证法的规律既用于研究社会和历史现象，也用于她自己的生活。马克思主义辩证法对她的知识分子身份尤为重要：作为一种概念工具，它允许她将生活划分为旧的和新的组成部分，关注它们之间的斗争，并在意识展开的辩证螺旋中挽救旧自我的有价值部分：

最近，一些大问题，甚至说是难题，变得特别尖锐。旧与新的问题是一个巨大的问题，足以耗费大量的思考和时间。那是因为这个问题可以用各种方式解决，而对我来说，它是这样的：如何（辩证地）将旧事物中好的、与我亲近的、属于我的、我从过去继承的（在血液中和通过教养获得的）、以及我曾经为之奋斗的部分——那古老而丰富的知识分子精神——与我周围和内心的新事物结合起来？我感觉到内心在世界观、对生活各方面的态度（特别是日常生活和道德问题，比如“三个字母”的例子……）方面萌发了某种新事物的强大嫩芽。但所谓的“新精神”有时包含了如此多庸俗、粗鲁和空洞的东西。这是不能接受的，是令人厌恶和反感的。一个人如何能够调和、统一、牢固而坚定地将属于我的旧事物与新事物联系起来？这可能吗？是的。过渡时期的产物——这就是我。
尽管帕夫洛娃对部分苏联官方文化的庸俗表现出厌恶，但这些保留意见并未削弱她拥抱共产主义理想及其所提供的（且唯有其能提供的）个人救赎诺言的决心。

While the teacher Vera Pavlova shared Olesha’s social background as the child of a factory manager, the narrative of self-transformation she sketched out in her diary exuded a confidence and resoluteness unknown to the ever self-doubting Olesha. An unquestioning believer in historical materialism, Pavlova applied the laws of Marxist dialectics to her own life as much as to the study of social and historical phenomena. Marxist dialectics were especially important to her intelligentsia identity: as a conceptual tool they allowed her to divide her life into old and new component parts, to follow the struggle between them, and to salvage valuable parts of her old self in a dialectical spiral of unfolding consciousness:

Recently some big questions, even problems, have become particularly acute. The problem of the old and the new is an enormous problem, capable of consuming a lot of thinking and a lot of time. That’s because this problem can be resolved in various ways, while for me it looks like this: How does one unite (dialectically) that part of the old which is good, which is close to me, which is mine, which I have from the past (in my blood and from my upbringing), and for which I used to strive—the old, rich intelligentsia spirit—with the new that is around and in me? I feel in me powerful shoots of something new in terms of worldview, my attitude toward various aspects of life, in particular, everyday life and moral questions (the example of the “three letters” . . .). But what is referred to as the new spirit sometimes contains so much that is vulgar, boorish, and empty. This cannot be acceptable, it is disgusting and repugnant. How can one reconcile, unite, link strongly and firmly that which is to be mine from the old and the new? Is that possible? Yes. A product of the transition period— this is what I am.

Even though Pavlova expressed revulsion at the vulgarity of parts of official Soviet culture, these reservations did not diminish her resolve to embrace the Communist idea and the promise of individual salvation that it—and only it—afforded.

当帕夫洛娃写下这篇日记时，一位年长的同事亚历山大·格奥尔基耶维奇·波列扎耶夫正在追求她，他执意邀请她去他家欣赏他的蝴蝶标本收藏。波列扎耶夫公寓里那种老式的舒适，在帕夫洛娃看来似乎自革命以来就没怎么变过，这让她想起了父母的家，也使她怀疑自己能否与波列扎耶夫建立关系。她尤其怀疑，与这个“旧知识分子”结合会否妨碍她实现入党的计划。与此同时，帕夫洛娃被另一位老师，一个叫杜尔凯特的人所吸引。她对两位追求者的比较显示，帕夫洛娃如何把自己所理解的分裂的知识分子自我投射到外部。

When Pavlova wrote this entry she was being courted by an older colleague, Alexander Georgievich Polezhaev, who insistently invited her to visit his home to admire his butterfly collection. The old-fashioned comfort of his apartment, which looked to her as if it had not changed much since the revolution, reminded Pavlova of her own parental household and made her doubt that she could have a relationship with Polezhaev. In particular she wondered whether a union with this “old intelligent” would allow her to pursue her plan of entering the Communist party. At the same time Pavlova was attracted to another teacher, a certain Dulkeit. Her comparison of the two suitors shows Pavlova’s externalization of what she conceptualized as her own divided intelligentsia self.

波列扎耶夫表现为一个“冷淡而迟缓的人，缺乏激情，对生活没有掌控力，宁愿退缩也不愿进入战斗”。更糟的是，他无法领导他的学生，他还抱怨他的教学职责，认为那只是“收入来源，仅此而已”。关于他的一切，无论是个人生活还是职业生活，都是彻头彻尾倒退的。“他对待当代事务、对待现有秩序的态度是负面的，断然负面的。”将波列扎耶夫具象化为一个“旧知识分子”，使帕夫洛娃得以辨认出自己内心残存的过时知识分子价值观，然后与之告别。相比之下，杜尔凯特体现了她所奋斗的新自我的本质。他显得“精力充沛、热情奔放、脾气火爆”，并全神贯注于工作。帕夫洛娃以典型的马克思主义方式结束了对杜尔凯特的评估，从他的个人美德转向其社会意义：“杜尔凯特在社会政治意义上也更新颖、更有生命力……他在本质上是一个当代人，他投身于生活，为之贡献精力，对其感兴趣。”

Polezhaev emerged as a “phlegmatic and slow person, who lacks fire, has no grip on life, and would rather retreat than enter a battle.” Even worse, he was unable to lead his students and he complained about his teaching duties, which he regarded only as “a source of income, not more.” Everything about him, his personal as well as his professional life, was deeply retrograde. “His relationship toward contemporary matters, toward the existing order is negative, decidedly negative.” Reifying Polezhaev into an old intelligent was a technique that allowed Pavlova to isolate, before parting with, remnants of outlived in-telligentsia values inside herself. Dulkeit, by contrast, essentialized the new self for which she strove. He appeared as “energetic, passionate, hot-tempered,” and engrossed in his work. Pavlova concluded her assessment of Dulkeit in good Marxist fashion, moving from his individual virtues to their social meaning: “Dulkeit is also newer and more vital in a sociopolitical sense . . . He is a contemporary in essence, he involves himself in life, devotes his energy to it, is interested in it.”
在她对这两个人的比较中（范围涵盖职业资格、职业道德、生活环境到音乐能力），帕夫洛娃拒绝比较他们的体貌特征，认为这不仅无关紧要，甚至是“庸俗的”（poshlo）。她对他们精神属性的强调旨在表明，她理解苏联秩序下的主体性首先是一种灵魂的品质，一种内在的气质。

尽管她在两个追求者之间摇摆不定，但她最终的选择具有一种预定的特质。几个月后她宣布“新与旧之间的斗争已随新事物的胜利而结束，因为新事物就是生活本身”，这便承认了这一点。但正如她在日记中明确表达的那样，这两个人都充当了一个超越他们任何一方的辩证项目的材料。她日记反思的最终焦点不在于男人本身，而在于她个人自我转型议程的辩证法。在她对追求者的众多比较中，有一次伴随着这样的评论：“不由自主地，产生了一种想要更深入分析，并因此想要写作的愿望冲动。”一旦她确定了她与这些人的关系的辩证基础，帕夫洛娃就在日记中不再提到他们。三年后的1935年，她嫁给了一位医学教授。

In her comparison of the two men, which ranged from professional qualifications, work ethics, living environment, to their musical abilities, Pavlova refused to compare their physical features, holding this to be not just irrelevant but even “vulgar” (poshlo). Her emphasis on their spiritual attributes was meant to suggest that she understood subjectivity in the Soviet order first and foremost as a quality of the soul, an inner disposition.

In spite of her vacillation between the two suitors, her eventual choice had a preordained quality. She acknowledged as much when announcing a few months later that “the struggle between the old and the new has ended with the victory of the new, because the new is life itself.” But as she also made clear in the diary, both men served as material for a dialectical project that transcended either of them. The ultimate focus of her diaristic reflections was not on the men themselves but on the dialectics of her personal agenda of self-transformation. One of her many comparisons of her suitors was accompanied by the remark: “Unwittingly, a flight of desire to analyze more deeply, and hence, to write.” Once she had identified the dialectical underpinnings of her relationships with these men, Pavlova made no further mention of them in her diary. Three years later, in 1935, she married a professor of medicine.

关于帕夫洛娃两个追求者的插曲，说明了她如何将与内在“旧人”的斗争外在化，并赋予“旧人”以物质现实。她在社会学意义上把像波列扎耶夫这样的人塑造成旧知识分子的典型，这使帕夫洛娃能够将自己塑造为新知识分子的一员。因此，她的推理指向了自我定义与对他人的社会定义之间一种有趣的相互作用。如果我们将这种机制应用于20世纪20年代和30年代广泛存在的告密行为，我们可以将告密理解为告密主体构建身份的行为。这是一种有代价的身份，因为它投下的影子形象——以旧知识分子或资产阶级敌人的形式——最终必须从苏联社会中切除。在帕夫洛娃的案例中，波列扎耶夫仅仅作为“过时”秩序的一员经历了象征性的死亡，而她的想法仅限于日记；然而，她构思这些想法时，针对资产阶级知识分子的告密行为正大量发生，且其后果是具体的，往往是致命的。

The episode surrounding Pavlova’s two suitors illustrates the way she externalized the struggle against the Old Man within and assigned the Old Man a material reality. Her sociological rendering of people like Polezhaev into epitomes of the old intelligentsia enabled Pavlova to fashion herself as a member of the new intelligentsia. Her reasoning thus points to an interesting reciprocal effect between self-definition and the social definition of others. If we apply this mechanism to the denunciatory practices that were widespread during the 1920s and 1930s, we can understand denunciations as acts of identity construction on the part of the denouncing subjects. It was an identity that came at a price, as the shadow image that it cast—in the form of an old intelligent or a bourgeois enemy—ultimately had to be excised from Soviet society. In Pavlova’s case, Polezhaev underwent merely symbolic death as a member of an “outlived” order, and her thoughts were confined to a diary, but nevertheless she formulated them at a time when the denunciations against the bourgeois intelligentsia were many and their consequences were material, often lethal.

与内在“旧人”的斗争渗透到了生活的各个领域，因为知识分子的每一个念头或行动都可以被解读为灵魂状态的表达。即使是像食物和日常琐事这样看似平凡的事情，也可以作为日记作者精神旅程的标志。苏联知识分子成员避免抱怨日常生活中的物质困难，要么对其保持沉默，要么将其称颂为他们成功自我更新的证据。在日记中，帕夫洛娃几乎没有提到20世纪30年代初极其艰苦的生活条件。最显著的是，她没有提到1933年的饥荒，她一定目睹了那场饥荒，因为那个夏天她在莫斯科附近的一个村庄度过。在20世纪80年代编辑她的日记时，帕夫洛娃评论说那是一个极其艰难的夏天，她曾多次被迫前往莫斯科寻找面包。但对于30年代的一位知识分子来说，压抑自己对食物等卑微事物的渴望是一种美德。相反，表达这种欲望，并进而质疑苏联国家的政策，就是暴露旧知识分子的自我。帕夫洛娃对波列扎耶夫最严厉的批评之一就是针对他对待食物的态度：“[他参与了]消极的反革命，伪装同化于新事物，但或许也在私下里幸灾乐祸和嘲笑。[他属于]那叹息过去（甚至包括食物）的旧知识分子，没有真正投身新生活，而只为它付出有限的精力。”

The struggle against the Old Man within pervaded all spheres of life, as every thought or action on the part of an intelligent could be read as an expression of the state of the soul. Even such seemingly mundane matters as food and daily chores could figure as signposts of the diarist’s spiritual journey. Members of the Soviet intelligentsia avoided complaining about the material difficulties of their daily lives, either passing over them in silence or hailing them as evidence of their success in renewing themselves. In her diary, Pavlova hardly alluded at all to the dire living conditions of the early 1930s. Most notably, she did not mention the famine of 1933, which she must have witnessed because she spent that summer in a village near Moscow. When editing her diary in the 1980s, Pavlova commented that this had been an extremely hard summer and that she had repeatedly been forced to travel to Moscow in search of bread. But for an intelligent during the 1930s, it was virtuous to repress one’s craving for such base matters as food. In-versely, to articulate such desires, and thereby to question the policies of the Soviet state, was to reveal the old intelligentsia self. One of Pavlova’s harshest criticisms of Polezhaev was occasioned by his attitude toward food: “[He engages in] the passive counter-revolution, faking assimilation to the new, but perhaps also gloating over and laughing in his sleeve. [He belongs to] the old intelligentsia, sighing for the past (even food), not joining the new life in earnest, giving it instead his energy only so far.”

这种评判也可以延伸到另一位日记作者，知识分子亚历山大·佩列古多夫身上，他遗憾自己没能在30年代记下一本“伟大的”日记。佩列古多夫的日记几乎完全围绕物质关注展开。他的年终总结显然缺乏自我反思。相反，它们以物资匮乏为中心：“1939年12月31日旧年的最后一天。消逝的一年几乎没有带来什么乐趣：几乎每个人都在贫困中；几乎每个人都在挨饿，没有衣服穿。一整年里，买衣服、鞋子和肥皂都要排长队。最近连黑面包也不够了。”同样，退休法语教师伊万·西奇全心全意认同俄国旧知识分子，并且没有表现出改造自我的倾向，他详细记录了各种消费品（如衣服、肥皂、黄瓜和避孕套）的稀缺和高价。这些态度正是《真理报》社论所指出的“右倾机会主义”反党运动的本质：它仅从供应的角度看待社会主义建设，“暴露了庸人完全狭隘的眼光，他缺乏历史远见，对周围发生的一切缺乏正确的理解”。

This judgment could have been extended to another intelligent, the diarist Alexander Peregudov, who regretted that he had not kept a “great” diary in the 1930s. Peregudov’s diary revolved almost exclusively around material concerns. His end-of-year summaries were conspicuously bereft of self-reflection. Instead they centered on the absence of goods: “12/31/1939 The last day of the old year. The waning year has brought few pleasures: almost everybody is in need; almost everybody is hungry and without any clothes to wear. During the whole year there were long lines for clothes, shoes, and soap. And lately there is not enough black bread.” Similarly, Ivan Sich, a retired French teacher who wholeheartedly identified with the old Russian intelligentsia and showed no inclination to transform himself, recorded in great detail the scarcity and high prices of diverse consumer goods, such as clothes, soap, cucumbers, and condoms.
