These attitudes were what a Pravda editorial identified as the essence of the “right opportunist” anti-party movement: it looked at the construction of socialism only from the point of view of supply, “betraying the complete narrow-mindedness of the philistine who lacks a historical perspective and a correct understanding of everything happening around him.”
苏联知识分子提及物质困难只有在服务于自我转型目的时才是合法的。例如，维拉·因贝尔在日记中自豪地详述她的艰辛，将其作为她新获得的力量的证据：

是的，前方有很多工作。如此艰巨的工作，难以置信地艰巨！好在我因为到处奔走、提着沉重的袋子、去佩雷德尔金诺的旅行，以及更清淡、脂肪更少的食物，身体变得更强壮了……我知道任何体力和脑力劳动的代价。我知道当你在蔬菜店，同时在三个队列里排队——在收银台、在接待处、然后是补交款项时，如何抑制自己的焦躁。你的脚痛，你的包裹散架了，你在胶布雨衣里热得要命，还有一只苍蝇粘在你的脸上，但你没法赶走它，因为你没有第三只手。

It was legitimate for a Soviet intelligent to mention material difficulties only if doing so served a self-transformative purpose. Vera Inber, for example, proudly detailed her hardships in her diary as evidence of her new-found strength:

Yes, there is a lot of work ahead. Such hard work, unbelievably hard! It’s good that I have become physically stronger from all the running around, hauling these heavy bags, the trip to Peredelkino, and the lighter, less fatty food . . . I know the price of any physical and mental work. I know how to restrain my irritation, when you are in a vegetable store, standing in three lines at the same time: at the cashier’s, at the reception, and then for the additional payment. Your feet ache, your parcels fall apart, your body is awfully hot in the oilskin coat, and there is a fly clinging to your face, but you can’t shoo it away, because you don’t have a third hand.

莫斯科一位工程学教授的妻子加琳娜·什坦格在日记中记录了当代生活的艰苦环境，以此来强调——并传达给后代——她那一代人在建设社会主义过程中做出的英雄牺牲：“1937年1月1日……当你想到现在人们是怎么生活的，特别是工程师，那真是太可怕了。我听说有一位工程师和他的妻子住在一间9[平方]米的房间里。当他的母亲来访时，他绝对没有地方工作。于是他把灯放在地板上，躺下（趴在桌子底下），就那样工作，他不能推迟工作，他有截止日期。我写下这个例子，是为了让后来者读到它，体会一下我们所经历的一切。”如果省略最后一句关于什坦格所针对的未来读者的内容，这段话读起来就会有所不同。她对生活条件的评论就会透露出绝望和政治批评。风险在于把某个陈述从其作为不可分割组成部分的更大叙事背景和策略中孤立出来。在苏联革命时期，这个背景是由转化和净化的叙事定义的；这些叙事支撑了因贝尔和帕夫洛娃对毅力的呼吁，它们也为西奇和佩列古多夫苍凉的陈述赋予了爆炸性的政治含义。

Galina Shtange, the wife of a Moscow engineering professor, recorded in her diary the difficult circumstances of contemporary life as a way to underscore—and to communicate to future generations—the heroic sacrifices made by her generation in the building of socialism: “1/1/1937 . . . It’s just horrible when you think about how people live these days, and engineers in particular. I heard about one engineer who lives with his wife in a 9-[square-]meter room. When his mother came to visit, there was absolutely no place for him to do his work. So he put the lamp on the floor and lay down (on his stomach under the table) and worked that way, he couldn’t put work off, he had a deadline. I wrote down this example so that those who come after us will read it and get a sense of what we went through.” This passage would read differently if the last sentence, on the future reader to whom Shtange addressed herself, were omitted. Her comment on living conditions would signal despair and political criticism. The risk is to present a given statement isolated from the larger narrative context and strategy of which it formed an integral part. In the Soviet revolutionary period this context was defined by narratives of transformation and purification; these narratives girded Inber’s and Pavlova’s calls for perseverance, and they also informed the bleak statements by Sich and Peregudov, lending them explosive political meaning.

在致力于铲除他们旧有的、资产阶级本质的同时，知识分子日记作者也积极参与了将苏联人口改造为新人和新女性的项目。这可能看起来自相矛盾，因为一个出身如此“不纯”的阶层，如何能将自己塑造为净化后人类的先驱？日记揭示了吸引知识分子成员采纳这一议程的两个主要动机。凭借其教育和文化储备，知识分子特别适合在布尔什维克国家中主张承担教导者的角色。启蒙“愚昧人民”的承诺早在革命前就已存在，并且是俄国知识分子职业和伦理使命中不可或缺的一部分。此外，他们作为“社会工程师”的角色，允许知识分子成员通过将其延伸到整个苏联领域，将他们个人对自我更新的追求外在化，并在此基础上获得认可和赦免。

While working to eradicate their old, bourgeois essence, intelligentsia diarists also actively participated in the project of remaking the Soviet population into new men and women. This may appear paradoxical, for how could a class of such “impure” origins cast itself as a progenitor of purified humanity? Diaries reveal two major motivations that drew members of the intelligentsia to adopt this agenda. Thanks to its reservoir of education and culture, the intelligentsia was singularly suited to claim a teaching role in the Bolshevik state. The commitment to enlighten the “dark people” long predated the revolution and was integral to the professional and ethical vocation of the Russian in-telligentsia. Moreover, their role as “social engineers” allowed members of the intelligentsia to externalize their personal quest for self-renewal by extending it throughout the Soviet realm, and on this basis to attain validation and absolution.

再教育的精神弥漫在帕夫洛娃的日记中。在莫斯科附近一个“沉闷、灰暗”且“落后”的村庄任教期间，她阐述了自己改造农民青年的艰巨使命。年轻的集体农庄工人只是表面上接受了她的教导，而他们身上“某种本能的、根深蒂固的东西”却在抵制她的“再教育”努力。在一个幽默的插曲中，帕夫洛娃总结了当时农村生活的现状：外表打上了革命的烙印，但在本质上仍渗透着落后。她的一位同事文化匮乏，几乎与普通村民无异，还给儿子取名为“十月”。帕夫洛娃不时会听到从这位老师家里传来的喊声，比如“十月！快从尿盆上下来！”或者“我的小十月死哪儿去了？”在日记的其他地方，帕夫洛娃带着显而易见的自豪感写道：“我传授知识，我教导如何工作，我培养新习惯，我在‘制造’人！……作为人的主人（哪怕他们只是青少年）是一种迷人的感觉……这种对自己和工作之意义的意识，这种综合，带来了满足感和热情。”在莫斯科“红火炬”工厂协助组织了一场艰巨的反对宗教运动后，帕夫洛娃以一种更恼火的口吻写道：“还需要多少时间和工作，才能将这群大众提升到社会主义国家真正公民的高度？……知识分子在这一任务中是多么必要啊。”作为一名苏联教师，她对自己那成问题的、带有部分资产阶级色彩的知识分子身份毫无顾虑，而在其他场合，这种身份曾引发如此多焦虑的反思。苏联知识分子被赋予的任务——担任新人的导师和抚育者，去像工程师一样塑造新人——证明了知识分子在自我更新的艰难探索中的合法性。

The ethos of reeducation suffused Pavlova’s diary. Teaching for a time in a “dull, gray,” and “backward” village near Moscow, she expounded on her daunting mission to remold the peasant youths. The young kolkhoz workers accepted her teachings only superficially, while “something instinctual, deeply ingrained in them,” resisted her efforts at “reeducation.” In a humorous episode Pavlova summed up the current state of village life, outwardly marked by the revolution, but in essence still permeated by backwardness. A fellow teacher, in her lack of culture almost indistinguishable from the rest of the villagers, had named her son after the October Revolution. Every so often Pavlova would hear shouts coming from the teacher’s house, such as “October! Get off the [chamber] pot!” or “Where the hell is my little October?” Elsewhere in the diary Pavlova noted with evident pride: “I give knowledge, I teach how to work, I train new habits, I ‘make’ people! . . . It is a fascinating feeling to be the master of people (even if they are only youngsters) . . . And this consciousness of your meaningfulness and the meaningfulness of your work, this synthesis, it causes satisfaction, enthusiasm.” After an arduous anti-religious campaign she had helped organize at Moscow’s “Red Torch” factory, Pavlova wrote in a more exasperated mode: “How much time and work will still be needed to raise this mass to the height of real citizens of the socialist state? . . . How necessary the intelligentsia is for this task.” In her capacity as a Soviet teacher she had no qualms about her problematic, partly bourgeois in-telligentsia identity, which had given rise to so much anxious reflection in other settings. The task assigned to the Soviet intelligentsia—to act as teacher and rearer of the new man, to engineer the new man—validated the intelligentsia in its own difficult quest to renew itself.

zh: 私人与公共，个人与社会
en: Private and Public, Personal and Social

children: 苏联体制的历史学家通常认为，只有私人表达的陈述才是个人“真实”信念的可靠指标。因此，他们赋予了作为私人记录之典范的日记一种独特潜力，使其能够以不失真的方式表达个人自我。相应地，源于公共领域的日记——如生产日记或旅队日记，或是为公之于众而写的记录——则被视为不真实的记录而遭到摒弃，特别是考虑到苏联国家施加的压力，迫使日记作者进行自我审查。

Historians of the Soviet system often assume that only privately voiced statements are reliable indicators of individuals’ “real” beliefs. They therefore endow the diary, understood as a private record par excellence, with a unique potential to express the individual self in undistorted fashion. Accordingly, diaries originating in the public realm— such as production or brigade diaries, or records written for the public eye—are dismissed as inauthentic records, especially in view of the pressures applied by the Soviet state, which forced diarists to practice self-censorship.

将公共-私人的二元对立应用于斯大林时代的日记和主体性，其问题在于，它将一种自由主义式的自我观投射到了苏联语境中。这种二元对立包含一个假设，即苏联公民像自由主义主体一样，追求个人自主，因此他们作为个人的自我表达，从定义上说就是在与社会或国家体制的张力中展开的。此外，自由主义模型提出了一个普世性的主张，即所有个人都将私人领域视为一个不受束缚且真实的个人主体性空间。然而，苏联日记作者对追求自主是否具有普遍性，以及私人领域是否是完整自我的领域，提出了质疑。私人与公共的概念，只要它们曾被用作苏联语境中的概念，就仍然有用，但重要的是要把握这些概念背后的历史特定含义及其用法。

The problem of applying a public-private binary to Stalin-era diaries and subjectivities is that it projects a liberal understanding of self-hood into the Soviet context. The binary contains an assumption that Soviet citizens, like liberal subjects, strove for individual autonomy, and that hence their self-expression as individuals by definition evolved in tension with social or state institutions. Furthermore, the liberal model makes a universal claim that all individuals cultivate the private realm as a sphere of unfettered and authentic individual subjectivity. However, Soviet diarists raise questions about the universality of the pursuit of autonomy and of the private as a realm of integrated self-hood. The notions of private and public remain useful to the extent that they were employed as concepts in the Soviet setting, but it is important to grasp the historically specific meanings underlying these concepts and informing their use.

在马克思主义的理解中，私人存在的概念助长了诸如个人主义、特殊主义和自私等反社会本能。此外，私人领域是维护资本主义制度的一种意识形态工具。它的功能是欺骗受压迫的工人，给他喘息之机，使他遗忘自己根本的异化状态。随着私有制的废除，社会主义革命将克服人类的自我分裂，并让人类重获其作为社会化物种的本质。在社会主义制度下，任何私人的观念都显得过时了。人从之前的资本主义压迫和自我分裂状态中解放出来，将恢复其作为社会存在的本性。根据马克思的说法，“首先应当避免重新把‘社会’当作抽象物同个人对立起来。个人是社会存在物。”未来社会主义社会的功能不是作为一种外部纽带，而是要表达人与人之间真正的内在统一。在摆脱了内在自我分裂和阶级冲突之后，新世界中的每个个人都将认同社会。

In Marxist understanding, the concept of a private existence furthered antisocial instincts like individualism, particularism, and selfishness. Moreover, the private sphere served as an ideological device that upheld the capitalist system. Its function was to deceive the oppressed worker, to give him respite and make him oblivious to his fundamental state of alienation. With the abolition of private property, the socialist revolution would overcome humanity’s self-division and allow humankind to regain its essence as a socialized species. Under socialism, any notion of the private was rendered anachronistic. Freed from his previous state of capitalist oppression and self-division, man would regain his nature as a social being. According to Marx, “what is to be avoided above all is the re-establishing of ‘Society’ as an abstraction vis-à-vis the individual. The individual is the social being.” The society of the socialist future was not to function as an external bond, but to express the real internal unity of men. Freed from internal self-division and class conflict, each individual in the new world would identify with society.

作为坚定的马克思主义者，布尔什维克不仅试图消除社会经济生活中的私有结构，还试图把苏联人口的意识从私人关切中净化出来。革命要占领人们生活的所有方面，特别是那些曾被认为是私人且非政治的领域。正如《共青团真理报》提醒苏联公民的那样：“日常生活并非私事，它是阶级斗争最关键的地带。日常生活与政治密不可分；那些在日常生活中不诚实、在道德上堕落的人，在政治上也是堕落的。”娜杰日达·克鲁普斯卡娅警告说：“私生活与公共生活的分裂，迟早会导致对共产主义的背叛。我们必须努力将我们的私生活与为共产主义而进行的斗争和建设结合起来。”

苏联要求个人过政治化的生活，根据社会效用来思考自己的存在，且不容许私人关切破坏其普遍主义取向，这一指令在当时的日记中表现得尤为明显。斯捷潘·波德卢布内反复提到他的“内在自我”（vnutrennost’）或“灵魂”（dusha）。他试图激活自我，并为之灌注苏联国家的革命议程。按照他的理解，苏联公民的灵魂应当充满鲜明的政治精神，并形成一个充满热情的领域。当他感到“内在一切都在沉睡”或徘徊在一种“愚蠢且非政治的情绪”中时，他感到不满。但当一种向政治领域升华的感觉贯穿他时，他满意地观察到自己的主观内在感受与客观社会世界的融合。同样，阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫也在日记中强调将个人生活与社会存在联系起来，他意识到，为个人事务本身而培养和记录个人关切，会暴露他是个庸人。他在写第一本日记本时就带有一种纲领性的精神，发誓要始终将他“个人生活”中值得记录的方面与他的“公共生活”联系起来：“我只生活在后者之中，我所有的个人利益几乎一直都与我的公共利益紧密相连。”然而，仅在几行之后，乌里扬诺夫就转换了话题，开始描述他的感情生活。他1930年代的大部分日记实际上都献给了他与女性的浪漫故事。然而，乌里扬诺夫一次又一次地责备自己的“小资产阶级”精神，决心摆脱卑微私人存在的纠缠，开始一种更高层次的、理性决定的生活。

As committed Marxists, the Bolsheviks sought not only to eliminate private structures in socioeconomic life but also to purify the consciousness of the Soviet population from private concerns. The revolution was to take hold of all aspects of people’s lives, and particularly of the realms that had been considered private and nonpolitical. As Komsomolskaya Pravda reminded Soviet citizens: “Everyday life is not a private affair, it is the most crucial zone of class struggle. Everyday life is inseparable from politics; and people who are not honest in everyday life, who are morally depraved, are depraved politically.” Nadezhda Krupskaya warned: “A division between private life and public life sooner or later leads to the betrayal of communism. We must strive to bind our private life to the struggle for and the construction of communism.”

This Soviet imperative that individuals lead politicized lives, think about their existence in terms of its social utility, and not allow private concerns to undermine their universalist orientation is markedly present in diaries of the period. Stepan Podlubny made repeated mention of his “inner self” (vnutrennost’) or his “soul” (dusha). He sought to activate the self and imbue it with the revolutionary agenda of the Soviet state. As he understood it, the soul of a Soviet citizen was to be filled with a distinctly political spirit and should form a realm of enthusiasm. He was dissatisfied when he felt that “all the inside is asleep” or when he lingered in an “idiotic and nonpolitical mood.” But when a sense of elevation toward the political sphere pervaded him, he observed with satisfaction the merging of his subjective, inner feelings with the objective, social world. Similarly, Anatoly Ulianov made a point in his diary of tying his personal life to his social existence, aware that a cultivation and reporting of personal concerns for their own sake would expose him as a philistine. He began his first diary notebook in a programmatic spirit, vowing to always link aspects of his “personal life,” to the extent that they deserved to be recorded, to his “public life”: “I only live in the latter, and all my personal interests are almost all the time tied in with my public ones.” Only a few lines later, however, Ulianov changed the subject and began to describe his love life. Most of his diary from the 1930s was in fact devoted to his romances with women. Yet time and again Ulianov chided himself for his “petit-bourgeois” spirit, resolving to overcome the entanglements of his lowly, private existence and to embark on a higher, rationally determined life.

事情并不只是说，苏联公民必须否认自身的个人一面，也不应在日记中讲述这些内容。日记作者建立的二元对立并不是个人与非个人、个人对社会或私人对公共。相反，他们试图在记述中避免任何此类二元模式。日记媒介本身倾向于单方面的、自我沉溺且潜在个人主义的自我叙述，他们则极力抵制这种倾向，他们极力强调自己身上具有政治意识、积极进取和社会化的特质。然而，这种强调并不排除与自我的亲密关系。乌里扬诺夫将日记当作私人朋友对待，习惯性地在条目结尾写下道别，并亲切地署名“托尔卡”（Tolka）。这位共青团积极分子从未想过要为自己对着日记说话时的那种亲密、甚至带有浪漫色彩的口吻而自责。对他而言，真正的问题在于他滥用日记作为宣泄虚弱、消极和唯我论本能的出口，有一次他甚至正式向日记道歉，因为他利用它来排解“无聊和忧郁”。
亲密感本身——如浪漫的梦想或家庭生活的片段——在意识形态上并不被视为应受谴责。相反，公民有权——且随着1930年代的推进，越来越多地被告诫——去培养他们的“个人生活”，这被视为社会主义文化变得多么人道和发达的标志。
公民在生产能力上越杰出，作为斯达汉诺夫式的劳动英雄或极地飞行员，他们的社会主义人格就被认为越发达，他们也就越应该追求个人生活。显然，在这些案例中，私人领域并没有与社会责任和欲望发生冲突，而是公民社会主义取向的又一种表达。

It was not simply that Soviet citizens were to deny any personal side of their existence and were not expected to narrate them in their diaries. The binary that diarists established was not one of personal vs. extrapersonal, individual vs. social, or private vs. public. On the contrary, they sought to avoid any such binary pattern in their accounts. Resisting the tendency inherent in the diary medium toward a one-sided, self-engrossed, and latently individualist self-narrative, they were at pains to stress the politically conscious, activist, and socialized qualities of their selves. This emphasis, however, did not preclude an intimate relationship with the self. Ulianov addressed his diary as a personal friend and habitually ended his entries with a farewell, affectionately signed “Tolka.” It never occurred to this Komsomol activist to reproach himself for the intimate, almost romantic tone in which he addressed his diary. To him the real problem was his abuse of the diary as an outlet for his weak, passive, and solipsistic instincts, and at one point he formally apologized to the diary for using it to discharge his “boredom and spleen.”

Intimacy as such—romantic dreams or episodes from family life— was not considered ideologically reprehensible. On the contrary, citizens were entitled and—increasingly as the 1930s progressed—admonished to cultivate their “personal life,” which was regarded as a sign of how humane and developed socialist culture had become.

The more outstanding citizens were in their productive capacities, as Stakhanovite heroes of labor or as polar pilots, the more developed their socialist personalities were assumed to be and the more they were to pursue their personal lives. Clearly in these cases the personal sphere did not clash with social commitments and desires but was one more expression of a citizen’s socialist orientation.

阿里阿德娜·奇尔科娃（Ariadna Chirkova）的日记很好地表达了这种对个人生活的新认可。奇尔科娃是一位32岁的莫斯科生物学家，她是一位被丈夫抛弃的单身母亲。她的幼子夭折了，留下她和一个年幼的女儿，除了日记，没有人能理解她的思想和感受，即她所有的“内心生活”。奇尔科娃嫉妒地评论了电台播送的一群在北极过冬的飞行员的消息。奇尔科娃注意到，报务员“如此担心他的家人，以至于他甚至提醒妻子各种不该忘记做的琐事：读某本书，订阅期刊，去剧院等等。我是一个怀疑论者，我不相信这一切……但我听着广播，又听到他妻子详细讲述全家人是如何度过这一天时，哭了。”奇尔科娃哭了，因为她在广播中听到的内容，无论是真实还是虚构，都提醒她自己没有这样的个人生活，她将其理解为一种嵌入更大英雄存在中的、充满爱、亲密和追求教育的家庭生活。

This new validation of personal life is well expressed in the diary of Ariadna Chirkova, a Moscow biologist. Aged 32, Chirkova was a single mother who had been abandoned by her husband. Her infant son had died and she was left with a young daughter, yet had nobody—except the diary—who would understand her thoughts and feelings, all of her “inner life.” Enviously Chirkova commented on a radio transmission from a group of aviators wintering at the North Pole. The telegraphist was, Chirkova noted, “so worried about his family that he even reminds his wife about all sorts of petty things she must not forget to do: read a certain book, subscribe to the journals, go to the theater, etc. I’m a skeptic, I don’t believe all this . . . But I cried, as I listened to the transmission and then to his wife’s detailed account of how the family had spent the day.” Chirkova cried because what she heard on the radio, true or fictitious, reminded her that she herself had no such personal life, which she understood as a family life of love, intimacy, and the pursuit of education embedded in a larger heroic existence.
相比之下，奇尔科娃日记中充斥的大量个人沉思必须被压抑，因为它们构不成一个完整的“个人生活”：

我的笔记随时随地都可能产生一种片面的印象。这只是我的内心世界。我的自我。但我只有在写这些笔记时，以及在一天中其他几个完全无关紧要的时刻才会沉浸在这个世界里。例如，在去实验室的路上。我其余所有的时间都被工作占据了。公共生活把我带走，让我完全入迷。对我来说，奋斗永远是第一位的。这些笔记对我来说只是一个小小的休息，除了对我自己，对任何人都没用，就在我喂伊罗奇卡（Irochka）吃李子或橘子的时候，我惊恐地想到成千上万、数以十万计的孩子根本没有这些东西。即便在我们的国家，这样的人仍然很多。

尽管奇尔科娃一开始强调私人领域——她日记的主题——对她的整体生活是多么微不足道，但她将这种内心生活与她的“自我”（ia）等同起来，从而暗示她的职业生活和社会记录对她的自我而言是外在的。似乎在写这条日记时，她意识到了自己选择的术语所暗含的危险，于是她急忙补充道，即使在最亲密的时刻，当她和女儿单独在一起时，她仍然心系普遍领域，并记得世界上“成千上万”不幸的、挨饿且缺乏良好母爱关怀的孩子。这条日记以引人入胜的细节揭示了那种鲜明的苏联式良知的机制，这种良知阻止一名苏联公民沉溺于她的个人生活，无论那生活是幸福还是不幸。
By contrast, the personal musings with which Chirkova’s diary abounded had to be repressed because they did not amount to a full-fledged “personal life”:

My notes always and everywhere can produce a one-sided impression. This is only my inner world. My self. But I am preoccupied with this world only when I am writing these notes, and during a few other, completely unrelated and insignificant moments in the course of the day. For example, on my way to the laboratory. All my remaining time is taken up with work. Public life carries me away and enthralls me completely. For me struggle always comes first. These notes are just a small break for me, of no use to anybody but me, when I feed Irochka plums or oranges and think with horror about the thousands, tens and hundreds of thousands of children who don’t have anything like that. And there are still many of those even in our country.

Although Chirkova began by underscoring how insignificant the personal realm, the subject of her diary, was for her overall life, she identified this inner life with her “self” (ia), thereby implying that her professional life and social record were extraneous to her self. It seems as if in writing this entry she became aware of the risky implications of her choice of terminology, so she hastened to add that even in her most intimate moments, when alone with her daughter, she remained committed to the universal realm and remembered the “hundreds of thousands” of unfortunate children in the world who were hungry and lacked good maternal care. In fascinating detail this entry reveals the mechanisms of a distinctly Soviet conscience that prevented a Soviet citizen from indulging in her personal life, happy or unhappy as it may have been.

奇尔科娃日记中提到的双重等级制度，即个人对社会、特殊对普遍，也出现在斯大林时代官方词典对“公民”一词的定义中：“社会的自觉成员，将个人利益服从于社会利益的人。”更广泛的社会关怀也高过纯粹的个人关怀，这体现在列夫·戴奇（Lev Deich）的日记中，他曾是一名孟什维克活动家，写日记时已年过七旬。戴奇将特定的日记条目分为两部分：他以“政治领域”的笔记开头，然后转向他的“个人领域”。在强调政治领域的“重大事件”时，他对自己的个人生活没有什么好话可说，称其为“不太好”，甚至是“恶心的”。同样说明问题的是，在第一个栏目下，戴奇使用的是集体代词“我们”（“我们正期待着从中得到各种好处”），而他的个人生活则在第一人称单数中展开。
“个人”和“国家”领域的地位不平等在列宁格勒高中生尼娜·索博列娃（Nina Soboleva）的日记中表现得淋漓尽致，她是当地一名高级党务官员的女儿。1940年1月，索博列娃被她的共青团支部提名，到列宁格勒的一家玩具厂担任“文化启蒙工作者”（kul’tprosvetrabotnik）。为了准备这项任务，她决心系统地阅读《真理报》，并记日记来记录和反思她的阅读。早先的一篇日记写道：

The double hierarchy addressed in Chirkova’s diary, of personal vs. social and particular vs. universal, also figures in the definition of the term “citizen” in an official Stalin-era dictionary: “a conscious member of society, a person who subordinates his personal to his social interests.” Broader social concerns also tower over the purely personal in the diary of Lev Deich, an erstwhile Menshevik activist who was in his seventies when he wrote the diary. Deich divided a given entry into two parts; he began with notes on the “political sphere” and then switched to his “personal sphere.” While emphasizing the “big events” of the political sphere, he had nothing favorable to report on his personal life, which he described as “not particularly good,” even “disgusting.” It is indicative, too, that under the first rubric, Deich used the collective pronoun “we” (“we are expecting all sorts of good things from this”), while his personal life evolved in the first person singular.

The unequal standings of the “personal” and the “state” spheres are illustrated glaringly in the diary of Nina Soboleva, a Leningrad high school student and daughter of a high-ranking local party official. In January 1940 Soboleva was nominated by her Komsomol cell to work as a “cultural enlightenment worker” (kul’tprosvetrabotnik) at a Leningrad toy factory. To prepare for the task she resolved to systematically study Pravda and also to keep a diary to record and reflect on her reading. An early diary entry said:

1940年1月13日
今天报纸上：
向斯大林同志致敬的洪流
欧洲战争。柏林。《科隆日报》撰文报道英法企图在北方发动战争。
巴黎……伦敦……国内新闻。“诽谤者纳波尔斯卡娅集团案”（关于该集团的反苏诽谤活动。所有五人都被判刑。纳波尔斯卡娅、伊万诺夫斯卡娅和戈罗霍夫各20年，米哈伊洛夫斯基和约诺夫各15年）。
好了，早上摘录完报纸后，我想写写我自己，但有一种奇怪的感觉——在记录了国家大事之后，再写各种个人的废话是多么尴尬。也许我该记两本日记？一本给社会领域，一本是个人的？

1/13/1940 Today in the newspaper: Stream of greetings for Comrade Stalin War in Europe. Berlin. The newspaper Kölnische Zeitung writes about the Anglo-French attempts to unleash a war in the North. Paris. . . London. . . Domestic news. “The case of the slanderous Napolskaya group” (on the anti-Soviet slanderous activities of the group. All five have received prison terms. Napolskaya, Ivanovskaya, and Gorokhov— 20 years each, Mikhailovsky and Ionov—15). Well, after excerpting the papers in the morning, I wanted to write about myself, but there was this strange feeling—how awkward to follow the chronicle of state affairs with all sorts of personal nonsense. Maybe I should keep two diaries? One for the social sphere, and one personal?
如果个人不能提升到政治的高度——这显然是索博列娃没想到的可能性——那么分记两本日记就可以防止政治文本被琐碎的个人关注所污染。

索博列娃和阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫都在日记计划开始时思考如何协调个人生活与社会活动家或苏联公民的角色。在写作过程中，他们意识到日记有潜力将他们引向一个支离破碎的、唯我论的、不适合苏联公民的“私人”世界，两人都对此做出反应，指出个人领域从属于他们的社会存在。但两人都没能在日记中维持国家语言的主导地位。就在上述日记写下仅两周后，索博列娃将她对《真理报》的解读缩减为一条标题，接着写道：“老实说，我今天不想读报纸。我最好写点关于我自己的事。”从这时起，她的日记变得越来越私人化，记录着她的友谊和青春期对父母权威的叛逆。日记开始一年后，新闻报道被放逐到了每条记录的末尾：“在结束之前，我想至少总结一下昨天的新闻报道……”

If the personal could not be raised to the level of the political—a possibility that apparently did not occur to Soboleva—keeping two different diaries would prevent the political text from being tainted by petty individual concerns.

Both Soboleva and Anatoly Ulianov began their diary projects with musings about how to reconcile their personal lives with their roles as social activists or citizens of the Soviet state. In the course of writing they became aware of the diary’s potential to steer them into a fractured, solipsistic, “private” world unsuitable for a Soviet citizen, and both reacted by pointing out that the personal sphere was hierarchically embedded in their social existence. But neither was able to sustain the predominance of state language in their diaries. Just two weeks after the entry quoted above, Soboleva reduced her exegesis of Pravda to a single headline and went on to write: “To be honest, I don’t feel like reading the newspaper today. I’d better write something about myself.” From this point on her diary became increasingly personal, chronicling her friendships and her adolescent rebellion against parental authority. A year after the diary’s inception the newspaper reporting was banished to the end of individual entries: “Before finishing, I want to at least summarize yesterday’s news reports . . .”

并非所有苏联日记作者在记录私密想法和梦境时都有矛盾心理。弗拉基米尔·热列兹尼亚科夫（Vladimir Zhelezniakov）作为村苏维埃主席，意识到自己有责任将个人关怀服从于社会利益：“1933年6月11日凌晨三点，我的妻子玛丽亚为我送行。见到她很好，但告别更难受。抛开所有个人利益，我大步走出，急忙去赶火车。我心里想的是皮罗戈夫村苏维埃。”然而，他并不羞于在日记中生动地描述一个私人梦境。他梦见了西班牙内战，看到自己把刺刀捅进法西斯的肚子里。然后他的妻子在床上翻身吵醒了他：“我很遗憾梦境被打断。也许我会看到英雄的马德里和著名的飞行员，击落敌机……英雄的西班牙人民的儿子们，我们与你们同在！法西斯主义将被打败！你，老婆，明天晚上翻身时小心点。我要去打击法西斯主义了。”热列兹尼亚科夫可以放心地在日记中讲述这个梦，是因为梦里完全充满了公共精神，因此不会威胁到他自我的统一。他甚至可能认为这是证据，证明他的潜意识已经成了他意识生活战场的延伸。民族志学家弗拉基米尔·比留科夫（Vladimir Biriukov）没有梦见西班牙内战；相反，战争本身，以及他对共和军每况愈下的担忧，让他度过了痛苦的失眠之夜。比留科夫和热列兹尼亚科夫都住在远离西班牙战场的偏远乡村，然而战争和国际阶级斗争在他们的生活记录中占据了重要地位。

Not all Soviet diarists had conflicting feelings about recording intimate thoughts and dreams in their journals. Vladimir Zhelezniakov, as chairman of a village soviet, was aware of his duty to subordinate personal concerns to social interests: “6/11/1933 At three in the morning my wife Maria saw me off. It was good to see her, but saying farewell was worse. Discarding all my personal interests, I stepped out briskly and hurried to catch the train. On my mind was the Pirogov village Soviet.” Yet he was not embarrassed to adorn the pages of his diary with the graphic description of a personal dream. He had been dreaming about the Spanish Civil War, watching himself running his bayonet into fascist stomachs. Then his wife moved in the bed, waking him: “I regretted my interrupted dreams. Perhaps I would have seen heroic Madrid and the famed pilots, shooting down enemy planes . . . We are with you, heroic sons of the Spanish people! Fascism will be defeated! You, Wife, be more careful when turning over tomorrow night. I will be fighting fascism.” Zhelezniakov could afford to narrate this dream in the diary because it was fully suffused with public spirit and therefore did not threaten the unity of his self. He might even have viewed it as evidence that his unconscious had become an extension of the battleground of his conscious life. Vladimir Biriukov, the ethnographer, did not dream about the Spanish Civil War; rather, the war itself, and his worries about the waning fortunes of the Republican army, caused him agonized, sleepless nights. Both Biriukov and Zhelezniakov lived in remote villages far from the Spanish battlefields, yet the war and the international class struggle assumed a strong presence in the chronicles of their lives.

诚然，并非所有苏联日记作者都渴望过一种完全专注于公共事务的典范生活，即使是那些渴望的人也几乎不可避免地达不到这一理想。尽管如此，个人与社会领域、特殊与普遍利益的分野，以及要求前者服从后者的律令，是大多数日记作者奉行的结构性事实。即使是具有批判思想的历史系学生阿卡季·曼科夫（Arkady Mankov）也曾写道：“1939年3月23日：一个人有两种生活：一种公共的，一种私人的[chastnaia]。迄今为止，这两者只有在少数幸运儿身上才和谐统一。对于绝大多数人来说，情况是这样的：如果一种生活不成功，他们就全身心地投入另一种生活。”尽管他诊断出了公共存在与私人存在之间的分裂，但曼科夫确实接受了包含公共与私人的统一自我的规范性观念。他哀叹苏联政权无法点燃他的主观精神，从而无法整合他的自我。在听到希特勒占领梅梅尔地区的消息后，曼科夫得出结论，他将不得不去打仗，却没有一个为之奋斗的意识形态目的。因此，即使像曼科夫这样的一位政权批评者，也坚持一种完整的自我理想，在这种理想中，个人将提升到社会的高度。

To be sure, not all Soviet diarists aspired to an exemplary life of exclusively public concerns, and even those who did almost inevitably fell short of this ideal. Nevertheless, the division between personal and social spheres or particularist and universalist interests, and the imperative to subordinate the former to the latter, were structuring facts that most diarists lived by. Even the critically minded history student Arkady Mankov once noted: “3/23/1939 A person has two lives: one public and one private [chastnaia]. To date the two have been harmoniously joined only in the case of a few lucky people. For the overwhelming majority it has been like this: if the one did not succeed, they gave themselves wholeheartedly to the other.” In spite of his diagnosis of the split between a public and a private existence, Mankov did accept the normative notion of a unified self embracing both the public and the private. He deplored the inability of the Soviet regime to kindle his sub-jective spirit and thereby integrate his self. Upon hearing of Hitler’s occupation of the Memel region, Mankov concluded that he would have to go to war without an ideological purpose to fight for. Thus even a critic of the regime like Mankov adhered to an ideal of an integrated selfhood in which the personal would be raised to the level of the social.

在思考私人情感与社会世界的关系时，其他几位日记作者区分了“小调”和“大调”。当日记中的声音是忧郁、压抑和沮丧时，他们将其描述为小调。这种孤独的曲调与这些日记作者归于苏联集体的嘹亮、整齐划一的欢呼声完全不同，也与他们自己希望体现的自信和力量的理想冲突。前侨民尼古拉·乌斯特里亚洛夫（Nikolai Ustrialov）回到莫斯科后，无法找到工作，也无法获得作为一名合格苏联公民的认可。他的绝望在他的日记中基本没有得到正面书写，却在一段描述年轻运动员列队穿过莫斯科的记录中表露无遗。那是他渴望归属的集体，它拥有他自己所缺乏的一切：“一群群、一队队青年，美妙的初秋阳光，扩音器里传出的管弦乐尖啸，还有那些声音——军事的、英勇的、大调的。奋斗、热忱、信仰和青春之歌。”阿列克谢·基里洛夫（Alexei Kirillov）是一名记者，因曾支持托洛茨基而被开除出共产党，他在日记中表达了他的绝望和频繁的自杀念头。然而，他一次又一次地敦促自己用一种乐观的“大调”来写作：“我会努力保持愉快，我正准备为争取留在党内的权利、为在这个地球上生存的权利而奋斗。”同样，当文学界官员亚历山大·阿罗塞夫（Alexander Arosev）的共产党员身份受到攻击时，他在日记中倾诉了忧郁的想法，同时希望切换到大调。在所有这些案例中，隐私都意味着一组孤独、矛盾、阴郁的感受，与公共生活嘈杂、充满活力和战斗性的合唱形成对比。

Several other diarists drew a distinction between “minor” and “major” keys when thinking about their intimate thoughts in relationship to the social world. When the voice in their journal was brooding, sub-dued, and depressed, they described it as in a minor key. Such lonely tunes were utterly unlike the resounding, unison cheer these diarists ascribed to the Soviet collective, and they also clashed with the ideals of confidence and strength that they themselves hoped to embody. After his return to Moscow, the former emigrant Nikolai Ustrialov was unable to find employment or to gain recognition as a full-fledged Soviet citizen. His despair, largely unaddressed in his diary, did come to the fore in an entry describing a parade of young athletes through Moscow. This was the collective to which he sought to belong, and it possessed everything that he himself lacked: “Cohorts and legions of youth, the wonderful early autumn sun, the orchestra scream of the loudspeakers, and the sounds—military, bravura, major. Songs of struggle, fervor, belief, and youth.” Alexei Kirillov, a journalist who had been expelled from the Communist party because of his one-time support for Trotsky, voiced his despair and his frequent suicidal thoughts in his diary. Yet time and again he urged himself to write in an optimistic, “major” key: “I will try to be cheerful, and I am preparing myself to fight for the right to be in the party, for the right to be on this earth.” Similarly, the literary official Alexander Arosev, when his credentials as a Communist were under attack, confided his melancholic thoughts to his diary while at the same time hoping to switch to a major key. Privacy in all these cases connoted a set of lonely, conflicted, and cheerless feelings, in contrast to the clamorous, vital, and militant chorus of public life.

一个相关的隐私概念是秘密领域。曼科夫在1938年注意到又有一群莫斯科大学的学生被捕了，但他正逐渐习惯这种情况，不再考虑自己可能被捕的可能性。“然而，”他补充道，“我有什么好担心的呢？到目前为止只有这些日记。”和曼科夫一样，斯捷潘·波德卢布内意识到日记中的秘密如果落入坏人手中会让他付出沉重代价，但他并没有停止写作。与此同时，他感到被自己的“黑暗想法”所污染和压抑，不断寻求释放。他对这个秘密空间没有积极的观念，无法在其中锚定一种有别于公共规范的自我认同和个人价值。因此，他并不认为他的日记是值得铭记的私人领域的记录。相反，它是一个“垃圾堆”，他可以将脑子里积累的所有“垃圾”丢弃在那里。他将写作想象成一场斗争，通过斗争他最终将得到净化，充满公共价值，并摆脱任何另类的、自私的、因而也是不纯洁的私人领域。

青少年时期的尼娜·索博列娃在父亲的书桌里找纸时，发现了一份可怕的文件：一份党内会议记录，会上她的父亲被指控在1937年和1938年检举了无辜的共产党员。根据文件，他通过坚称这些人是真正的人民敌人来为自己辩护。索博列娃不知道该相信什么。她写道：“在无意中读了父亲的文件后，一种沉重的感觉笼罩在我体内的某个地方（‘在心里’？‘在灵魂里’？）。”索博列娃指责自己犯下了那个时代最严重的政治罪行之一，宣称她对父亲秘密的了解已将她变成了一个“两面派”：一个外表上苏联式的人，内心却藏着违反苏联真诚准则的秘密。她采取的解决办法是停止在那本被污染的日记本上写作，把它藏在安全的地方，再换一本新的。她将日记描述为非法且会连累自己的思想的存放处，这表明她将秘密领域视为革命纯洁和透明理想的阴暗面，是苏联争取最大限度光明所创造出的一个阴暗角落。在一种无所不包的净化热忱背景下，这是一种非法的隐藏姿态——然而它并不是（或至少当时还不是）积极自我认同的源泉，也不是自主思考传统引以为傲的奠基时刻。

A related notion of privacy was the sphere of the secretive. Mankov noted in 1938 that yet another group of Moscow University students had been arrested, but that he was getting used to this situation and no longer thinking about his own possible arrest. “However,” he added, “what do I have to worry about? So far only the diaries.” Like Mankov, Stepan Podlubny was aware that the secrets in his diary would cost him dearly if it fell into the wrong hands, yet he did not stop writing. At the same time, he felt polluted and weighed down by his “black thoughts” and kept seeking a release from them. He had no positive notion of this secret space in which to anchor a sense of self and personal values diverging from public norms. Therefore he did not conceive of his diary as a record of a private sphere to be remembered. Rather, it served as a “rubbish heap” on which he could discard all the “garbage” that accumulated in his mind. He envisioned writing as a struggle from which he would ultimately emerge cleansed, suffused with public values, and rid of any alternative, selfish, and hence impure, private sphere.

While searching for paper in her father’s desk, the teenaged Nina Soboleva discovered a terrible document: a record of a party meeting at which her father had been accused of having denounced innocent Communists in 1937 and 1938. According to the document, he had defended himself by maintaining that these had been real enemies of the people. Soboleva did not know what to believe. She wrote: “After this inadvertent reading of father’s papers a kind of heavy feeling has settled somewhere inside me (‘in my heart’? ‘in my soul’?).” Accusing herself of one of the most serious political offenses of the period, Soboleva declared that her knowledge of her father’s secret had turned her into a “double-dealer”: a person outwardly Soviet, but with an inner secret that violated the Soviet mandate of sincerity. The solution she adopted was to stop writing in the polluted diary notebook, hide it in a safe place, and continue with a fresh notebook. Her description of the diary as a repository of illicit and compromising thoughts suggests that she looked upon the realm of the secretive as a dark obverse of the ideals of revolutionary purity and transparency, a dark recess created by the Soviet striving for maximum light. It was an illegitimate gesture of concealment in the context of an all-embracing purificatory zeal—yet it was not (or not yet) a source of positive self-identity or the proud founding moment of a tradition of autonomous thinking.

“隐私”这个概念本身并没有普世意义。它获得正面还是负面的评价取决于自我表达所在的意识形态背景。在苏联的案例中，鉴于革命国家推崇公共和集体主义精神，个人记日记并不是为了培养一种与公共领域相对立的私人存在，这或许并不奇怪。因此，将自由主义倾向的公共-私人二元对立应用于此，并假设私人领域是积极认同的所在，对于理解苏联主体性并无用处。这并不是说日记作者没有详细阐述他们的私生活：他们详细叙述了私密的梦境、幻想和浪漫际遇，报告了家庭问题，并记录了某天所吃的食物等平庸事实。然而，他们中的许多人责备自己滑入了这种“小资产阶级”或“个人主义”的叙述模式，认为它在苏联文化中不被认可。最重要的是，这种与公共价值和公共利益脱节的私人想法威胁到统一完整人格的理想，因此当日记作者开始反思自我的质量时，这些想法遭到了否定。几乎没有一本日记在推崇自主、自足和个人主义的个人理想。许多日记之所以私密，是因为其中藏有作者小心防止他人窥探的秘密；但这些秘密思想并未被系统地发展为私人身份认同。

The concept of “privacy,” as such, has no universal meaning. It acquires positive or negative valence depending on the ideological context in which the self articulates itself. In the Soviet case, given the public and collectivist ethos promoted by the revolutionary state, it may be not surprising that personal diaries were not kept to cultivate a private existence in contradistinction to the public sphere. Thus the application of the public-private binary in its liberal inflection, with the assumption that the private realm forms a locus of positive identity, is not useful for an understanding of Soviet subjectivities. This is not to say that diarists did not expound on their private lives: they narrated at length their intimate dreams, fantasies, and romantic encounters, reported on family problems, and recorded such mundane facts as the food they ate on a given day. Yet many of them chided themselves for sliding into such a “petit-bourgeois” or “individualistic” mode of narration, which they held to be illegitimate in Soviet culture. Most important, such private thoughts, disconnected from public values and public interest, threatened to undermine the ideal of an integrated personhood and were therefore repudiated when diarists began to reflect on the quality of their selves. Hardly a diary promoted personal ideals of autonomy, self-sufficiency, and individualism. Many were private in the sense of harboring secrets that their authors carefully guarded from intrusive glances, but these secretive thoughts were not systematized and extended into private identities.
日记作者并非使用私人和公共的二分法，而是根据社会和普遍的公众利益来定位他们的个人和特殊存在。这些描述唤起了两种轨迹——个人狭小有限的主观生活，以及体现历史客观进程的集体生活——理想情况下，两者应融为一体。日记作者一次又一次地写下他们努力将个人生活融入苏联集体的“生活总流”中。

有别于集体生活甚至与之对立的私人存在被认为是低下的、未实现的。集体被想象成一个活生生的、有呼吸的身体，是苏联自我实现的终极目的地。在加入集体时，个人的自我变得步调一致并得以扩大。个人与集体的关系在意义和提供共同体感的能力上，极大地超越了与另一个人的任何关系。阿纳托利·乌里扬诺夫曾一度中断了他对卡佳（他无法赢得她的心）和加利娅（她的主动示好让他无动于衷）的“孤独”沉思，宣称他实际上爱的是党，他需要党，党也同样需要他。他在一个革命节日里恰如其分地表达了他的誓言，几个月后乌里扬诺夫加入共产党，这一誓言也随之圆满兑现。

Rather than using the dichotomy of private and public, diarists situated their personal and particular existence with respect to the social and general public interest. These descriptions evoke two trajectories— the small and limited subjective life of the individual, and the life of the collective, embodying the objective course of history—which ideally were to coalesce into a single whole. Time and again, diarists wrote of their efforts to merge their personal lives with the “general stream of life” of the Soviet collective.

A private existence in contradistinction or even opposition to the life of the collective was considered inferior and unfulfilled. The collective, imagined as a living, breathing body, was the ultimate destination of Soviet self-realization. In joining a collectivity the individual self became aligned and enlarged. An individual’s relationship with the collective vastly surpassed any relationship with another person in meaning and the ability to furnish a sense of community. Anatoly Ulianov at one point broke off his “lonely” musings about Katya, whose heart he could not win, and Galya, whose advances left him cold, by declaring that he actually loved the party, who needed him as much as he needed her. His vow, fittingly expressed on a revolutionary holiday, was consummated some months later, when Ulianov joined the Communist party.

虽然集体的成员身份有力量抵消苏联公民“个人生活”中的不幸（也见奇尔科娃的日记），但失去这种身份会产生彻底的孤独感。这在尤利娅·皮亚特尼茨卡娅（Julia Piatnitskaya）的案例中表现得非常强烈，她不得不看着以前的熟人疏远她，她的儿子们也失去了朋友。她得出结论：“不幸有某种气味”，她和儿子们正散发出一种即使每天洗澡也洗不掉的气味。有时皮亚特尼茨卡娅甚至感到与自己的孩子疏远。当她向16岁的大儿子吐露她那“邪恶、有毒”的怀疑，即他们正处于一个残忍而专断的国家体制手中时，他会责备她：“妈妈，这种时候我觉得你很恶心，我真想杀了你。”她还引用11岁的小儿子的话说：“真遗憾他们没枪毙爸爸；毕竟，他是人民的敌人。”为了重新加入革命共同体并克服她在社会中的孤立，皮亚特尼茨卡娅必须谴责她的丈夫就是“人民的敌人”。这就是她求助的国家检察官所建议的。皮亚特尼茨卡娅日记的大部分内容都在描述她感到多么“痛苦”，因为她无法鼓起力量去恨她的丈夫，从而无法恢复她作为苏联公民和社会主义集体成员的意识形态上的合格身份。

While membership in the collective had the power to offset personal unhappiness in a Soviet citizen’s “personal life” (witness also Chirkova’s diary), losing this membership could engender total loneliness. This showed powerfully in the case of Julia Piatnitskaya, who had to watch as former acquaintances turned away from her and her sons also lost their friends. She concluded that “misfortune has some sort of smell,” and that she and her sons were emitting an odor that would not wash off, in spite of daily baths. At times Piatnitskaya even felt estranged from her own children. When she confided to her older son, aged 16, her “evil, poisonous” suspicion that they were in the hands of a cruel and arbitrary state system, he would reproach her: “Mama, I find you disgusting at times like this, I could kill you.” She also quoted her younger son, aged 11, as saying: “It’s too bad they didn’t shoot Papa; after all, he is an enemy of the people.” In order to rejoin the revolutionary community and overcome her isolation in society, Piatnitskaya had to denounce her husband as just that: an “enemy of the people.” This was what the state prosecutor, to whom she turned for help, suggested. Much of Piatnitskaya’s diary describes how “tormented” she felt because she could not muster the strength to hate her husband and thus restore her ideological credentials as a Soviet citizen and member of the socialist collective.
